text:
One of the joys, or perils, of a weekly Tuesday newsletter is coming out every year on Election Day, right when the world is on hold for those 13 or so hours the polls are open. If you live, as I do, in a corner of Pennsylvania without a hotly contested congressional race, and with Gov. Josh Shapiro up by double digits, the day might seem less consequential. That’s wrong. Not only is control of the state legislature on the line, but we’re fighting for a bigger principle: the right to vote again in a free and fair election in two years. Vote as if your life depends upon it, because in a sense, it does.

In Maryland, a man named Julian Curo Churata arrived more than a decade ago from Peru to work as a carpenter and build a new life with his wife, Veronica Ramirez, their two children from previous marriages, and eventually their own daughter, now age 6.

In June, as President Donald Trump's campaign of mass deportation was surging across America, agents from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested Curo Churata in a targeted operation, and the undocumented immigrant was flown to detention in Louisiana. He managed to call his daughter every day—pretending he was out of town on a job—until September 29, when ICE said he suffered cardiac arrest, was rushed to a nearby hospital, and pronounced dead. He was just 47.

The most despicable campaign promise in American history proved to be the only one Trump kept.

Ramirez went public with her grief, her unanswered questions about her husband’s death, and the lack of information she was receiving from ICE, in a story on the front page of The Washington Post.

“He wasn’t a criminal,” Ramirez said at the time. “All he wanted to do in this country was work. He paid his taxes, he wanted a better future for his children and for me—for his family. He didn’t deserve this at all. I want justice.”

What Ramirez got instead from ICE was a notice to appear for an immigration court hearing that could lead to her deportation to El Salvador—dated just three days after the newspaper article. Now she fears for the future of her already traumatized daughter, who may lose a second parent. “She’s afraid—afraid of being alone,” Ramirez said.

This case of seeming retaliation by an uncaring and increasingly tyrannical US government where the ultimate victim is a defenseless 6-year-old girl is the kind of article that makes your blood boil. But it’s also just one of a series of stories of heartlessness and violent thuggery toward the undocumented on our soil that have polluted my social media feed in recent days.

I saw a video of an ICE agent pointing a gun in the face of an innocent bystander in North Hollywood, California during the arrest of an immigrant; read about the Afghani refugees that ICE plans to fly back to their native country even after their relatives risked everything to aid US troops; and noted the Cuban-American lawyer who voted for Trump in 2024, tried and failed to stop his cousin’s deportation during the ensuing ICE crackdown, and then cried that, “This isn’t what I voted for.”

No, this is exactly what you voted for. I was inside Milwaukee’s Fiserv Forum on the night of July 16, 2024—watching in horror as white Trump delegates in their red MAGA garb or Texas cowboy hats waved placards that read, “MASS DEPORTATION NOW.” The most despicable campaign promise in American history proved to be the only one Trump kept.

And you still don’t think that elections have consequences?

There are millions of people—who live on our blocks, and pray in our houses of worship, and work the backbreaking jobs in our communities that no one else seems willing to do—who face the greatest consequences from the results of Tuesday’s midterm election. People like Veronica Ramirez and her 6-year-old girl.

Our neighbors with the most to gain or lose from the election results, for whom Tuesday’s election is about a lot more than paying a few cents less per gallon at the gas pump, are also people who cannot vote.

They desperately need you to cast a vote for them.

Hubert Humphrey, the former Democratic vice president known for his outspoken defenses of civil rights in the postwar era, said most famously that “the moral test of government is how that government treats those who are in the dawn of life, and those who are in the shadows of life...”

In today’s United States, no one is forced to retreat into those shadows more deeply than the 14-million-or-so undocumented immigrants and the American dreams of their children, many of whom are US citizens who might have to watch masked government goons rip their parents away.

Unfortunately, it’s a nightmare that won’t end on Wednesday morning no matter who wins, since Trump and his xenophobic henchmen like Stephen Miller will still be in the White House and—barring the unexpected—will be there until January 20, 2029.

But your vote will still make a huge difference. One party will hold public hearings, subpoena top officials, expose evil, and refuse to provide any new dollars to co-opt our local police to arrest our neighbors, hire more masked thugs, or open the squalid equivalent of concentration camps. The other party will continue, and look to expand, a mass-deportation crusade that has become a dark moral stain on our nation.

It’s fine to vote your pocketbook, but Tuesday’s ballot is about so much more. This is a moral imperative.

I know when I vote Tuesday, I’ll be thinking about Wendy Martínez, a woman I met this summer in Pottsville. With her four kids, Martínez rarely left their cramped apartment with the windows covered in blankets after ICE took away her husband, Carlos Moreno. There are thousands like her—women whose family breadwinner was arrested by ICE in a deliberate strategy to drive their families out of the United States.

Martínez won’t be voting Tuesday, but you can.

I think about the family members like Maryland’s Ramirez or Ly Wang, the stepdaughter of a Philadelphia Amerasian immigrant from Vietnam named Tuan Van Bui. whose loved ones died this year in the ICE-detention gulag archipelago, with little or no explanation

Ramirez won’t be voting Tuesday, but you can.

Tuesday’s election caps a year that started with the brutal murders by immigration officers in Minneapolis of two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who objected to what the government is doing in our name.

Good and Pretti won’t be casting ballots on Tuesday, but you can. If you care about justice, you must.

Many are. Tuesday morning, I woke up to see a photo online of the ever-growing memorial to Pretti on the Minneapolis street corner where the protester was gunned down nine months ago. A number of Minnesotans have traveled straight from their early-voting site to the memorial, and attached their “I Voted” stickers.

You can play a role in ending the erosion of gains for Black and brown Americans in the classroom and the voting booth; turning the tide back toward the LGBTQ community, including our transgender neighbors; and electing more opponents of US militarism from Iran to the Caribbean.

title: ICE agents cause a scene at Santa Barbara County Jail
description:

text:
PORTLAND Ore. (KPTV) - A federal judge has determined that federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have repeatedly failed to follow his order requiring a warrant before an arrest is made in Oregon. In one case, the judge determined an agent lied about having a warrant.

The judge released a 50-page opinion on the matter. The order was issued in February.

The judge discussed several arrests as evidence of the defiance. In one case, he determined an ICE agent lied on official documents.

That arrest took place in July. A man identified only as “HDGH” was on a trip with a friend in Ashland.

The agent testified he was running license plates and got a hit on the friend, who had a warrant for being in the United States illegally. The agent followed the two and eventually arrested both.

The agent said both men had warrants. HDGH said agents did not know who he was. The agent then said he made a mistake and that his testimony was false.

In the arrest record, known as an I-213, the agent said agents had a warrant for HDGH. The agent later admitted they did not. He said he “wrote it as if I already knew who the person was, but I did not.”

The judge wrote in his opinion: “It defies logic that such consequential errors in the I-213 form are merely a mistake.”

Based on the testimony of the agent and HDGH, the judge determined the agent intentionally lied.

The judge is ordering the agency to meet new reporting requirements to show compliance with his ruling. He is ordering ICE agents to provide unedited documents and body camera footage of all arrests.

Since the injunction blocking warrantless arrests in February, ICE agents have made more than 500 arrests in Oregon. Attorneys representing the federal government say only 15 of those arrests were warrantless.

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security have been asked for a response to the ruling. This story will be updated when a response is received.

text:
One Friday this past June, a man who lived in The Dalles with his wife and kids was making Walmart deliveries in Hood River. From the parking lot, he collected an order and left to bring it to the customer. Then, a federal judge recently wrote in a summary of the encounter, about six U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement vehicles surrounded the man. They told him to get out of his vehicle, handcuffed him and put him inside their own.

These officers did not, the judge wrote, ask the man questions, show paperwork, or declare they had a warrant, but as they drove along, they began making inquiries and checking his ID. After two hours by some train tracks in the Columbia River Gorge, the agents then drove the man to a secluded parking lot in Portland—at which point, after another two-hour wait, another ICE vehicle drove up, an agent forced the arrested man to sign paperwork without explaining what it was, and took him to Tacoma, Wash., where he remained for nearly the entire summer until, in mid-September, a judge in Washington state got him out.

As it turned out, the judge concluded, the ICE agents seem to have taken the wrong man.

When the arrestee, who in court papers is identified only by the initials JCCV, got some of ICE’s paperwork, it turned out that it described the vehicle of his brother, not his, and misstated the location of the arrest, claiming it occurred near Napa, Calif.

This story of a man “appallingly” detained for several months because of ICE’s errors was one of several that U.S. District Judge Mustafa T. Kasubhai recounted in a blistering Monday ruling as evidence of the sloppiness and lawlessness with which the agency has been arresting people in Oregon over the past year.

The Eugene federal judge has evidently lost patience with the agency, which he has now ordered to supply drastically more documentation of its work—including body camera footage of all civil immigration arrests in the state of Oregon—after he found that agents routinely violated his past orders, lied in at least one case, and showed incompetence in many more.

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment. But the agency has argued the judge was hamstringing their efforts to enforce federal immigration law.

Moreover, the case of JCCV demonstrates how convoluted and contradictory the U.S. immigration system has become for millions of people. According to court papers, JCCV came to the U.S. more than three years ago, was arrested but released and granted temporary protected status, had that status revoked last year, but retains a pending asylum claim and authorization to work in the U.S.

While ICE, Judge Kasubhai pointed out, did not offer any testimony to contradict the man’s account of his apparently accidental arrest, JCCV’s is the sort of immigration status that the Trump administration has routinely characterized as “illegal,” and the agency argued his arrest was justified.

Kasubhai rejected this argument, and his scathing order adds his voice to the mounting chorus of judges who have found the Trump administration and its agents to be unreliable narrators of events.

Where courts would generally give the benefit of the doubt to a public agency, the judge writes, ICE has broken trust. Its many errors, he wrote in his order Monday, “prove that, without external accountability or supervision, ICE is not capable or competent in conducting its investigative and enforcement activities with integrity.”

The case in question, M-J-M-A v. Wamsley, originally centered specifically on the matter of a Woodburn woman whom ICE arrested in late 2025. But it soon expanded into a class action case, representing a broad range of people ICE has arrested in Oregon without a warrant.

Making an arrest without a warrant is not forbidden in itself, the judge writes, but it tends to require certain predicates, like probable cause and concern that the person would flee. To ensure these conditions were in fact met, Kasubhai in February ordered ICE to record the circumstances of its warrantless arrests and provide the plaintiffs with basic documentation.

At the time, the judge wrote, he believed the disclosure of a particular form (called the I-213 narrative) would be sufficient for plaintiffs to monitor whether ICE was complying with the law. But 500-plus ICE arrests later, “evidence of Defendants’ poor recordkeeping has changed the Court’s stance,” he wrote, noting that ICE has failed to report all of its warrantless arrests, and those reports it did submit were inadequate. “The I-213 narratives produced by Defendants in this case have been boilerplate, vague, or outright fabricated.”

Indeed, the judge’s 50-page order began by describing an ICE officer admitting to falsely stating facts in documentation as the basis for an arrest. This was, the judge noted, the only ICE officer who had testified in the case, and “there is no telling how many other agents in Oregon engaged in similar misconduct, which calls into question the veracity of all I-213 forms completed by ICE officers in Oregon.”

For these reasons and others, the judge set down new terms. ICE will have to remind its agents of his orders every 30 days. It cannot redact documents (“the Court has little confidence that Defendants will comply with any instruction that would allow some redaction,” he wrote), and it will have to produce more documentation overall. This, he wrote, would include all body camera footage of civil immigration arrests in the state of Oregon.

Judge Kasubhai made clear one of his goals was to produce a robust evidentiary record. “This case,” the judge wrote, “underscores what happens if people were not called to testify under oath in a courtroom, if as a society we do not demand that government agents explain their actions, and if the public fails to shine a spotlight on what is happening under cover.”

text:
The Santa Clara County Sheriff’s Office began restricting access to Elmwood Correctional Facility in Milpitas on Friday amid increased federal immigration enforcement outside the jail, citing public safety concerns.

The restrictions apply to federal organizations as well as members of the public without approved jail-related business. People picking up someone being released from custody will no longer be allowed into the parking lot and must arrange a pickup outside the restricted areas, authorities said.

People released from custody can voluntarily wait in the jail’s lobby until daylight, the Sheriff’s Office said. But community advocates questioned whether barring family pickups from the grounds would leave those leaving custody exposed to immigration arrests.

“The jails should be facilitating the least restrictive way for people to pick up a loved one who’s being released to take them home and out of any dangers that are lurking outside,” Raj Jayadev, co-founder of advocacy group Silicon Valley De-Bug, said of the new policy.

The new policy follows two incidents outside the jail last week: an incident on Wednesday night after which a man was hospitalized after being tased by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers and one on Friday night in which a volunteer monitoring ICE activities and three ICE agents were treated at a local hospital.

Community advocates have also said that agents near the jails have started to question people about their immigration status instead of carrying out targeted arrests.

The Sheriff’s Office referenced “several recent incidents near the facility” that “created safety concerns and operational challenges in areas used by employees, visitors, individuals being released from custody and members of the public” but did not specifically reference last week’s ICE encounters, according to a news release from the Sheriff’s Office. That “increased activity” around the facility “has affected traffic flow” and “raised concerns about the safe movement of vehicles and pedestrians,” the Sheriff’s Office added.

“Our responsibility is to maintain a safe and secure environment for everyone who comes to Elmwood, including staff, visitors, service providers and those leaving our custody,” Sheriff Bob Jonsen said in the news release. “These changes are intended to improve safety, reduce disruptions and ensure the facility can continue operating effectively while respecting the rights of all individuals.”

The restrictions limit entry and exit to one location on the jail’s west side at 945 Thompson Street, authorities said. Visitors must show an ID to enter the parking lot. On Monday morning, sheriff’s vehicles were parked to block other entrances around the jail’s perimeter, and orange traffic barriers blocked most of the primary entrance where a sheriff’s deputy checks the IDs of those entering.

Authorities added that the restrictions will “apply equally to all individuals and local, state, and federal organizations seeking entry to the facility grounds.”

Approved reasons to enter include attorneys visiting their clients at the jail, those going for planned visitation and those with approved jail-related business, including contractors and service providers, authorities said.

For those picking up someone being released, the Sheriff’s Office is encouraging them to “identify a safe pickup location outside the restricted areas.”

Those released from custody will be allowed to wait in the lobby, said Brooks Jarosz, senior communications officer for the Sheriff’s Office.

“For your safety, if you are released from jail late at night or early in the morning, the Sheriff’s Office encourages you to stay in the Elmwood lobby until daylight. This may be especially helpful if you do not have a ride arranged,” reads a notice posted in the lobby shared by Jarosz. “After you are released, you are no longer in custody and are free to leave at any time. Staying in the lobby is completely your choice, but is strongly encouraged when it is nighttime.”

The notice adds that snacks, water and phone chargers are available, and that those who do not follow the lobby rules will be asked to leave.

“Once it is light outside, please leave as soon as you can,” the notice continues.

The new restrictions will remain in place indefinitely, Jarosz added.

The Santa Clara County Rapid Response Network expressed appreciation for the Sheriff for “seeing what is happening and adjusting their policies to minimize risk to releasees and community members and responders who have volunteered to support the releasees.”

“However what has been proposed is not enough,” the network said in a statement Monday. “Closing public access to federal agents, community members, and even the family of those who are being released means they just walk out of the facility to be questioned and picked off by federal agents who are post there in the late night/early morning hours. The Sheriff needs to do more to protect releasees and their families, particularly when people are being released at night.”

Santa Clara County’s sanctuary policies restrict local law enforcement’s assistance with civil immigration enforcement. The county has also established “ICE-free” zones on county property, but agents have previously used publicly available inmate release lists and then waited outside of the facility to detain individuals.

“Consistent with California law and County policy, the Sheriff’s Office does not assist ICE with civil immigration arrests, honor civil immigration detainers, or notify ICE when individuals are being released from custody,” the office said in an FAQ about the new policy. “The new facility access restrictions do not change these longstanding policies.”

In the East Bay, Orinda officials confirmed that ICE arrested a person in the city Friday. Members of a community group said agents made the arrest in front of a child and left the child behind, but city authorities did not immediately confirm that account.

In a statement posted on social media, city officials said they confirmed with ICE that “federal agents were conducting a targeted effort on an individual with a criminal arrest warrant. The arrest occurred in Orinda.”

City officials said ICE told them it was an isolated incident and there were no ongoing enforcement activities in the city. ICE did not respond immediately to requests from this news organization for comment.

text:
In the upcoming midterm elections, 50 million Gen Z Americans are eligible to vote, making up 20% of all eligible voters.

In 2024, Gen Z voters represented the lowest voting turnout (only 20 million voters out of 40 million eligible), many current polls show that Gen Z is more motivated than ever this midterm season.

This election season, there are many key issues young American voters are motivated by, including the economy, human rights and the current presidential administration.

Concerns about a worsening economy

As young voters are living on their own for the first time, they are increasingly concerned about the higher cost of living, a worsening job and housing market and an incredibly expensive healthcare system.

“Everything’s too damn expensive. Nobody has any money. The job market is s*** for young people,” Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.) said. Frost is currently the first and only Gen Z member of Congress.

AI-driven job displacement is also a concern among young voters. A poll from the Harvard Kennedy School shows that nearly 64% see AI replacing jobs as a serious threat to their financial security.

As the American Dream feels out of reach for Gen Z, many will vote for candidates that vow to lower affordability costs.

Trump administration

Many of the voting groups that helped President Trump win in 2024, including Gen Z male voters, are instead turning to the Democratic party in the midterms.

Nearly, 88% of Gen Z voters said that corruption is important to their midterm vote.

“Corruption is a top concern, reflecting profound distrust in fundamental democratic institutions. As they feel current policies fall short, young people are turning toward populist economic ideas and candidates who actively respond to the crises they face,” said Sophie Robertson, the student chair of the Harvard Public Opinion Project.

Aggressive immigration tactics

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has been a hot topic all over the country, especially in places with large immigrant populations.

Nationwide, Gen Z has led the cause in advocating for immigrant rights, including through boycotts and protests. Last spring, DU students organized a gala to fund a local Denver nonprofit, Casa de Paz.

Polls have also found that Gen Z attitudes towards ICE are negative, with only 38% of voters agreeing that ICE makes them feel safer, while 48% disagree, including 39% who strongly disagree.

With the killings of civilians by ICE, Americans are generally more skeptical of ICE’s aggressive enforcement tactics. This skepticism is expected to show at the polls.

Election Day is Nov. 3. If you’re a DU student who has not yet casted their ballot, the in-person voting center on DU’s campus is located in the multipurpose room at Diamond Family Residential Village, 2020 S. High St.

text:
Welcome to the weekly Free Movement newsletter!

The Home Secretary is expected to set out the details of the government’s earned settlement reforms in a Commons statement today, alongside its response to the public consultation. Last week, cross-party MPs and civil society organisations wrote to the Home and Health Secretaries, warning that doubling or tripling the qualifying period for settlement risks a repeat of the Windrush scandal and would worsen staff shortages in health and care.

A ministerial statement and policy guidance was published on the three refugee sponsorship routes: named community sponsorship, refugee study and refugee work. Community groups, universities and employers will be able to sponsor people already recognised as refugees, with the first arrivals expected from autumn 2027.

Open Rights Group has published a report on how the Home Office uses artificial intelligence, from estimating the age of people seeking asylum to summarising interviews and flagging suspected sham marriages. It says these tools are being rolled out in ‘near total secrecy’ and are reinforcing bias and discrimination. It calls for regulation and a public register of government AI tools.

Asylos is asking for input to help scope its next thematic country of origin information research project, including priority topics, countries and other information gaps that affect asylum and protection decisions. The survey closes on 13 November. Its latest report, published in June, examines human trafficking in Vietnam.

Over on the blog, Zaki Sarraf has looked at whether the government is legislating against a caricature of article 8. Clause 19(4) of the Immigration and Asylum Bill would require decision makers to give ‘no weight’, rather than ‘little weight’, to private life or relationships formed while a person was in the UK unlawfully. That raises the question of how far Parliament can dictate the outcome of the proportionality assessment.

We also have the new UK practice toolkit on climate, disasters and protection claims, which was launched by Earth Refuge and Refugee Legal Support. The toolkit shows practitioners how climate and disaster factors can be built into existing asylum and human rights arguments.

Finally, we’ve updated our explainers on age assessments and section 3C leave.

text:
Key events

It has just gone past 06:30 in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia where polls have now opened.

Share

Updated at 06.42 EST

What are some of the key issues in the midterms?

Here are some of the key voter issues shaping the US midterm elections:

The economy: Despite Trump’s 2024 campaign pledge to tackle affordability issues, the economy consistently ranks as voters’ top concern.

Iran: Trump’s decision to go to war with the Tehran regime has exacerbated economic worries. Iran’s retaliatory decision to close the strait of Hormuz has driven up gasoline prices for US motorists. It also represents a breach of his pledge to end the US’s supposed addiction to “forever wars”.

Immigration: Enforcement and closing the border remains a signature issue for Trump. He repeatedly boasts of the impact of his closure of the southern border as one of his biggest achievements, making comparisons with the performance of Joe Biden.

AI and datacenters: AI has emerged as a key campaign issue, with surveys showing a majority of voters holding negative views on it, even as Trump champions its development and attempts to rename it “super intelligence”.

You can read more about the issues guiding the elections here:

Share

Updated at 06.20 EST

Robert Tait

A final set of polls from the New York Times and Siena University, published on Sunday, put Democratic candidates ahead in five of seven key battleground contests – including Texas and Kansas, where voters have not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1988 and 1932, respectively.

The final stretch of the campaign was not without drama for the Democrats, however. In Michigan – widely seen as a crucial pillar to either party’s ambitions of control in the Senate – Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost her party’s senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, on Sunday.

Stevens was widely condemned by fellow Democrats over the move, which followed a feud with the El-Sayed campaign over an outside group’s campaign ad that blamed the high cost of living on US support for Israel. Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, described her endorsement of Rogers as “a despicable betrayal”.

“Whatever they’re trying to distract you, it’s because they’re picking your pocket,” El-Sayed told hundreds of supporters in Royal Oak, Michigan on Monday.

The extraordinary rupture in Michigan took places days after the party faced damaging headlines in Alaska, where it was reported that the Democratic senate candidate’s campaign was behind an effort to recruit a challenger with almost the same name as her rival, the Republican senator Dan Sullivan. (The Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, has denied any knowledge of such a scheme on the part of her campaign.)

Before the report of the Peltola campaign’s involvement, the Department of Justice (DoJ) filed a lawsuit to block the certification of Alaska’s Senate results in the event of a Republican defeat, citing potential “voter confusion” over the presence of two Dan Sullivans on the ballot. The lawsuit has since been dismissed by a judge.

Share

Updated at 05.59 EST

When will we know who has won?

David Smith

Voting is taking place today (Tuesday 3 November), but the results may not be known tonight. Close contests, different state rules for counting early and postal ballots, and possible recounts or legal challenges could delay the final outcome.

Once the dust has settled, there will be no respite in this – the land of the endless campaign. Attention will soon turn to the 2028 presidential election campaign, when both parties will seek to turn the results of this November into a foundation for the next fight for the White House.

Here’s an hour-by-hour rundown of when polls close around the US, courtesy of our blogger and reporter Shrai Popat:

Share

Updated at 05.37 EST

First polls open in US midterm elections

The first polls have opened in the pivotal US midterm elections in the eastern state of Vermont, where it has just gone past 5.15am.

The next polls to open will be at 6am ET (in 40 minutes) including in: Connecticut, Indiana, Kentucky, Maine, New Jersey, New York and Virginia.

The first results will start to come in after 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT) but a tight race could take hours to call – or even days.

It is important to remember that more than 58m early votes have already been cast across the US, according to an analysis by the University of Florida, a huge increase in the total number of early votes made in the last midterm elections, in 2022.

Share

Updated at 06.40 EST

Rachel Leingang

Rachel Leingang, a Midwest political correspondent for Guardian US, has been in Iowa, getting a sense of the political mood ahead of the crcuial elections:

Across Iowa on Monday, candidates made final pitches in a set of toss-up races up and down the ballot, noting just how close these contests were and how pivotal the state could be for the nation’s politics.

In a standing-room-only town hall in Waverly, Iowa, Democratic gubernatorial hopeful Rob Sand started off by asking people in the crowd which political party they belong to, then having people clap for all of them before directing the audience to sing “America the Beautiful” together.

The bipartisan tone underscores Sand’s pitch to Iowa voters, including those who would need to cross party lines to support him: “not redder or bluer, but better and truer”.

Wearing shirts that urged people to vote for Democrats and “rotate the crops”, about 150 voters turned out to the rally in the Republican-leaning area. Sand told the Guardian that throughout the hundreds of town halls he has seen a “yearning” from people for their politicians to work together to solve problems, even as voters are generally angry this year.

“We need to focus that anger and point it at where it ought to be pointed, which is at a broken two-choice political system that is too easily abused to allow elected officials to be corrupt and to be lazy and still hold power,” he said. “A lot of politicians want people to be angry with their neighbors.”

Down in the Des Moines suburbs in the early evening, as rain poured down and the sun set before 6pm, Sarah Booz knocked doors for Democratic candidates. On the doors, there were still a lot of undecided voters.

Some told her they’d be voting for Sand and the rest of the downballot Democrats, while others said they needed to do more research. One man who said he normally votes red said the gubernatorial race would probably be a last-minute decision.

And in the evening, at a Holiday Inn by the Des Moines airport, much of the Republican ticket rallied, culminating in a pitch from US Senate candidate Ashley Hinson. Chuck Grassley, the Republican US senator and the oldest sitting US senator, took digs at Sand, saying that the state government is well run and “we don’t need Sand in that machinery”. He also called Democrats running across the country “outlandish socialists” who want to “transform America”.

What is being decided in the midterms and why do they matter?

David Smith

The US Congress has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate. Both must approve federal legislation before it can become law and both play important roles in overseeing the executive branch.

The House is elected every two years, meaning all 435 voting seats are contested at every congressional election. The Senate has 100 members serving staggered six-year terms, so roughly a third of its seats are up for election every two years.

This year’s ballot includes:

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives. Republicans are defending a narrow majority, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.

35 seats in the Senate. Thirty-three seats are up in regular elections, along with two special elections in Florida and Ohio to fill the remainder of terms that were vacated early. Republicans currently hold 53 seats, against 47 held by Democrats and independents who caucus with them. Democrats need to gain four seats to secure a majority.

39 governorships. Voters will choose governors in 36 states and three US territories.

Thousands of state legislative seats, as well as local offices, judicial contests and ballot measures on issues including taxes, abortion rights and voting rules.

The elections for Congress will determine which party controls Congress for the final two years of Trump’s second term. The governorships and state legislative contests will shape policymaking closer to home, from education and reproductive rights to taxation and the administration of elections.

The midterms have a long history of punishing the occupant of the White House. The president’s party has lost House seats in 18 of the past 20 midterm elections, a 90% rate of loss that stretches back to 1946.

What are the races to watch in the US midterm elections?

David Smith

in Washington

Donald Trump will still be US president on the morning of 4 November. But he could be facing a very different political landscape, depending on the results of the midterm elections held the previous day.

As the name implies, midterm elections fall nearly halfway through a president’s term. They are often a telling referendum on the sitting president’s performance, something Trump is actively encouraging by telling voters “pretend I’m on the ballot”. In this case, voters will decide whether Trump’s Republican party can retain its grip on Congress.

Democrats are hoping to capitalise on growing discontent with Trump to seize control of the US House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate. Republicans are fighting to preserve their congressional majorities and prevent a fresh period of legislative paralysis and investigations into the White House.

Several Senate contests have emerged as key battlegrounds. In Michigan, progressive Abdul El-Sayed is seeking to hold an open seat for Democrats against Republican Mike Rogers, who received a last-minute endorsement from Democrat Haley Stevens. In Georgia, Jon Ossoff, a Democratic senator, enjoys a healthy poll lead over Republican challenger Mike Collins.

In Maine, a state won by Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, Susan Collins, the Republican senator, is defending her seat against Democrat Troy Jackson. Ohio offers another major test, with Democrat Sherrod Brown seeking to return to the Senate against Republican Jon Husted.

Texas has become especially closely watched. Democrat James Talarico is taking on Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general. Republicans have spent about $210m to help the scandal-plagued Paxton. No Democrat has won a statewide election in Texas since 1994. Trump won Texas by nearly 14 points in 2024.

In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate race against Republican incumbent Dan S Sullivan sparked controversy after Republicans accused the candidate of planting a second Dan Sullivan to confuse voters. A judge dismissed a Trump-backed lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s Senate race results if Dan Sullivan loses.

Other contests in Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and New Hampshire could help determine which party controls the chamber (if there is a 50-50 split, JD Vance, the vice-president, a Republican, wields the tiebreaker vote). Latest polls show Democrats ahead in Maine, North Carolina and Kansas, and competitive in Ohio. Also on the map this year are South Carolina and Mississippi, two reliably Republican states that have seen aggressive Democratic challenges this year.

It’s Tuesday 3 November, which means that after months of campaigning, debate and analysis, the critical US midterm elections that will take the political temperature of the nation halfway through Donald Trump’s second term – and determine the trajectory of the remainder of his presidency – are finally upon us. With the US president almost unprecedentedly unpopular, Democrats are aiming for what would be stunning victories in seats where, for decades, turning blue would have been unthinkable. Trump is not on the ballot, but this election is very much a referendum on the direction of the country under his Republican party.

Trump’s agenda has thrown the US into a deeply unpopular – and expensive – war alongside Israel against Iran, sparking a global energy crisis and regional conflict that remains unresolved. The war has exacerbated inflation and the cost-of-living crisis, which had already been worsened by Trump’s chaotic tariff policies. text:
The vote counts from key Senate, House, and gubernatorial elections around the country.

After months of hard-fought campaigning, the midterm elections have finally arrived. Today, voters are heading to the polls to decide which party will control Congress, and to cast their votes in several consequential gubernatorial races around the country. Recent polling suggests that the Democrats are likely to wrest control of the House of Representatives back from Republicans, and they have a shot at the Senate, where the G.O.P. currently holds a fifty-three-to-forty-seven vote advantage. The most likely path for Democrats to take the latter includes defending seats in three key swing states—Michigan, New Hampshire, and Georgia—and flipping at least four of seven competitive Republican-held seats: Alaska, North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Maine, Kansas, and Texas. The first polls will close tonight at 6 P.M. Eastern Standard Time, and The New Yorker will publish results, as reported by the Associated Press, until the final votes are tallied.

This year’s midterms will go down as the most expensive election ever—including past Presidential cycles—as more than eleven billion dollars has been spent on campaign advertising alone. The bulk of this spending has been concentrated on a handful of Senate races, with more than a billion dollars going to just three states: Michigan, Ohio, and Texas. Texas, in particular, is considered a major bellwether for the Democrats; the state representative James Talarico holds a narrow polling lead over Texas’s attorney general, Ken Paxton, despite President Donald Trump winning the state by more than thirteen points in 2024. If Talarico wins—becoming the first Democrat elected statewide since 1994—it will likely be because of Latino voters, who polls suggest, after swinging sharply toward the G.O.P. in 2024, have moved back to the left. It will also reflect a deep dissatisfaction with Trump, whose approval rating has sunk into the thirties—recently hitting the lowest point in either of his two terms.

Accordingly, Democratic candidates have actively sought to make the election a referendum on Trump, and, across several recent polls, voters have rated issues related to the President as their top priorities. This has included Trump’s war in Iran, which has contributed to high inflation and spiking gas prices, and data-center construction, which Trump has championed. If the Democrats are able to take back Congress, Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the presumptive Speaker of the House, has signalled plans for aggressive oversight, including congressional investigations into business deals by figures close to the Trump Administration, immigration-enforcement reform, and potentially even impeachment hearings. The results of today’s midterm elections could also offer a preview for the 2028 Presidential landscape, providing an early test for several potential Democratic nominees who are currently up for reëlection in their respective states, such as the Maryland governor, Wes Moore; the Pennsylvania governor, Josh Shapiro; and the Georgia senator Jon Ossoff.

Throughout Election Day, and into the night, The New Yorker will provide live updates on election results, with reporters filing dispatches from battleground states nationwide and columnists offering fresh analysis as votes start to come in. Sign up for our daily newsletter for continued coverage in the days following the election, and subscribe to The Political Scene Podcast for in-depth post-election interviews and analysis.

text:
Federal data show a dramatic slowdown in naturalization approvals ahead of today’s Nov. 3 midterm election, leaving hundreds of thousands of potential voters in New England and across the U.S. in limbo.

Application approvals through the first eight months of this year are down more than 70% compared to the same period last year.

Lucia Martel Dow, director of the New Americans Campaign for the Immigrant Legal Resource Center, said some people fear they may be targeted for deportation if they even apply.

“People may have no reason why not to apply for naturalization but seeing what is happening in their neighborhoods or people that they know, may definitely make them think twice of whether this is the right time to apply or they want to sit it out,” Martel Dow observed.

Last month, a Department of Homeland Security social media post celebrated the decline in naturalization approvals and increased deportations as part of its mandate for “remigration,” a far-right term used for the removal of non-white immigrants.

A recent poll of more than 1,000 naturalized citizens by the National Partnership for New Americans found 78% believe immigration enforcement has gone too far.

Nicole Melaku, executive director of the partnership, said while 90% of those surveyed expressed a commitment to vote, disinformation regarding voter fraud and stepped-up immigration raids have left them feeling uneasy. She noted an alarming 53% are questioning whether it is safe to cast a ballot.

“I think a lot of folks are sort of computing basically the threat versus the reward and to not be dissuaded from fully participating at this time given what’s at stake,” Melaku explained.

The Trump administration recently announced a $25 million program to encourage the public to report suspected immigration fraud, including voter fraud, to the Department of Justice. Meanwhile, Democratic members of Congress have asked the administration to explain why numerous naturalization ceremonies have been repeatedly canceled or delayed.

They said people have spent years complying with immigration requirements to become U.S. citizens and exercise the given rights, including voting, obtaining a passport or petitioning for family members.

text:
The former chief of the FBI's Chicago Field Office said he was forced out of his job after he said he was wrongly blamed for the failed prosecution of six people who protested against the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in the Windy City, according to a lawsuit he filed on Monday.

Douglas DePodesta sued top Justice Department officials, alleging that federal prosecutors pushed "politically motivated prosecutions" against Chicago demonstrators before gathering evidence, according to the lawsuit. He said his superiors notified him that FBI Director Kash Patel pushed for his ouster before he was forced to resign over the summer.

"I saw the writing on the wall," DePodesta told The Associated Press.

DePodesta accused the top federal prosecutor in Illinois, U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois Andrew Boutros, of launching a "campaign" within the DOJ to blame him after the so-called "Broadview Six" case fell apart earlier this year.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION HAS LOST OR ABANDONED HUNDREDS OF LAWSUITS AGAINST ANTI-ICE PROTESTERS, MIGRANTS: REPORT

Hours after the lawsuit was filed, U.S. District Judge April Perry ordered Boutros and three of his assistant attorneys to testify under oath on Nov. 16 in the failed "Broadview Six" case.

"There is more than an adequate factual basis for the Court to pursue an inquiry as to whether willful false statements were made to the court," Perry wrote in the order.

Federal prosecutors brought charges against roughly 30 protesters during the federal immigration enforcement operation in Chicago, dubbed Operation Midway Blitz, but many of those charges have since been dropped or dismissed.

DePodesta’s lawsuit alleges that Boutros faced pressure from the DOJ throughout the immigration crackdown to slap protesters with felony charges.

"Boutros sent DePodesta emails demanding that DePodesta open FBI investigations into individuals with political views or affiliations in opposition to the Trump administration," DePodesta’s attorneys wrote in the complaint.

Boutros often pressured assistant U.S. attorneys to press charges "before investigating the objective evidence," according to the lawsuit, which says he wanted felony charges when assistant U.S. attorneys "favored misdemeanors or no charges at all."

Last October, Boutros charged six people with conspiring to obstruct a federal officer, a felony, in connection with their actions during a protest at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in the Chicago suburb of Broadview.

Grand jury transcripts later turned over to the court showed that grand jurors twice declined to indict the six people as prosecutors sought charges, according to The Associated Press. Boutros dropped all charges against the six people in May as the court moved to investigate possible prosecutorial misconduct.

Boutros "repeatedly complained to his superiors in Washington" that the failure was DePodesta's fault "to deflect attention from his own malfeasance," DePodesta's attorneys wrote in the lawsuit.

DePodesta denied Boutros’ claims to his superiors at the FBI, and they conceded that he was only being forced out of his job due to the "political pressure Boutros created," according to the suit.

The complaint alleges Boutros told DOJ leadership that DePodesta and his sister-in-law, Nancy DePodesta, who is an attorney representing one of the six former defendants, "conspired to destroy" the case.

PRITZKER CALLS FOR CRIMINAL INVESTIGATIONS INTO ICE AGENTS OVER ‘MIDWAY BLITZ’ CONDUCT

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"There is no one at the FBI who took their oath of office and their ethical and moral responsibilities more seriously than Doug," Nancy DePodesta said in a statement to The Associated Press, adding that it is "both heartbreaking and shameful that he was forced out of his position based on what appear to be utterly false rumors spread by" Boutros.

In September, one of the prosecutors on the "Broadview Six" case abruptly resigned, writing in a resignation letter that Boutros had "scapegoated and publicly vilified" her. She filed a motion asking the court to treat her as an independent party moving forward.

The former defendants have asked the judge to appoint a special counsel to probe possible misconduct by prosecutors. At an Oct. 1 hearing, Perry ordered further "fact-finding" about communications between Boutros’ office and DOJ leadership.

Boutros has previously denied that politics played a role in charging decisions.

Fox News Digital reached out to the DOJ for comment.

title: Sen. Alex Padilla and Rep. Jim Costa turned away from ICE detention facility in McFarland
description:

Several families from across the Central Valley have told Action News their loved ones have been held at Golden State Annex.
ICE's Office of Detention Oversight inspected Golden State Annex June 23-25.
Padilla said this was not the first time he has been denied access to an ICE facility and that he plans to return.
text:
MCFARLAND, Calif. (KFSN) -- U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla and U.S. Rep. Jim Costa made an unannounced visit Monday to Golden State Annex in McFarland, saying they wanted to inspect conditions inside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility amid what they described as a surge in immigration enforcement across California.

"I've lived in this Valley all my life. I've never, never seen the level of fear that we see today over the last two years that has, I think, purposely been created by this administration: fear of going to work, fear of going to school, fear of going shopping," Costa said.

Padilla and Costa spent about 50 minutes at the facility before leaving. They said a supervisor at Golden State Annex, which is operated by the private company GEO Group, told them ICE staff from Fresno needed to be present before access could be granted and that their arrival could take at least a couple of hours.

"It's unacceptable, and it's insulting. For members of Congress trying to do our job, he could not point to a section of the law. He could not point to a section of their contract that prohibited him from granting us access so we could do our job," Padilla said.

"It became very clear he's just trying to stonewall us," Padilla said.

In a statement released after the visit, Costa said the lawmakers "were denied access to basic information and given the runaround."

"As members of Congress, we have a constitutional right to conduct oversight of these facilities and ask basic questions about the conditions, medical care and treatment of detainees," Costa said in the statement.

The visit comes as Padilla says more than 60 people have died in ICE custody since President Donald Trump returned to office. That compares with 26 deaths reported by ICE during President Joe Biden's four years in office.

"Their refusal to grant us access to the detention facility raises serious questions about what they're trying to hide," Padilla said in a statement.

According to GEO Group's website, Golden State Annex can hold up to 700 people. ICE's most recent inspection report says the facility holds men.

The facility opened in 1997. Until March 2020, it was a private prison that held state inmates under a contract with the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation. The state ended that contract as part of its exit from for-profit prisons, and ICE began housing detainees there that same year.

ICE deportation officers are not assigned to the facility full time. According to the inspection report, they make scheduled visits once a week, on Tuesdays.

Several families from across the Central Valley have told Action News their loved ones have been held at Golden State Annex.

ICE's Office of Detention Oversight inspected Golden State Annex June 23-25. According to the report, facilities like this one are notified four weeks before an inspection.

Inspectors identified seven deficiencies. Inspectors found one detainee received a required health assessment, including a mental health screening, 20 days after arriving, rather than within the required 14 days. In two cases, staff took six and seven days to respond to detainee grievances, beyond the five-day standard.

One detainee told inspectors he had a fractured foot and had not been scheduled to see a specialist. According to the report, he first reported foot pain May 6. An X-ray on June 16 showed a fracture, and his podiatrist appointment was still pending when inspectors left.

The report also found that none of the 18 detainees interviewed alleged discrimination, mistreatment or abuse. The facility's rating improved this year to "Good," up from "Acceptable/Adequate" in 2025, and its number of deficiencies dropped from 17 to seven.

"These are people that overwhelmingly have committed no violent crime. These are not the worst of the worst. These are people that would be addressed if we were to fix a broken immigration system," Costa said.

"ICE has been consistent in their unwillingness to be transparent, to be forthcoming," Costa said.

Costa said that when he visited Mesa Verde last year, he gave a week's advance notice because he wanted to meet with detainees from the Fresno area who had contacted his office. He said that when he arrived, those detainees were no longer there.

Padilla, the ranking member of the Senate Judiciary Immigration Subcommittee, has conducted oversight visits to immigration detention facilities and holding centers across California, including facilities in California City, Otay Mesa, San Francisco International Airport, downtown Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Diego.

"I've lost count of how many visits throughout the state of California and beyond, through Texas, all the way to Guantanamo Bay," Padilla said.

"There was a lot of questions we were ready to ask. The question we're leaving with is, what do they have to hide?" Padilla said.

Padilla said this was not the first time he has been denied access to an ICE facility and that he plans to return.

"It will definitely be a return visit. Scheduled or unscheduled, we don't know yet," Padilla said.

"I will keep showing up, demanding answers, and fighting to ensure the law is followed and people's rights are protected," Padilla said in a statement.

text:
In its latest request to the Supreme Court over President Donald Trump’s approach to immigration, the Justice Department turned to the court’s emergency docket to ask for fast-track permission to construct a border barrier system along a 517-mile stretch in remote west Texas. Stymied by a federal district court’s preliminary injunction issued in October, the Justice Department argues that Supreme Court intervention is needed to prevent irreparable harm to the country. But details of the government’s legal argument reveal that the Trump administration hopes to use the emergency docket as a fast track to victory regardless of the actual urgency of the legal dispute.

Early this year, the Department of Homeland Security began taking important preliminary steps to build physical barriers through Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, and nearby property along the U.S.-Mexico border. Part of the Border Patrol’s Big Bend Sector, covering approximately one-quarter of the entire border, no artificial barriers exist there. Despite its massive geographic reach, the region is sparsely populated and at immense distance from large urban centers. Unlike other parts of the U.S.-Mexico border, few people or goods cross from one country to the other in the Big Bend Sector. Indeed, according to U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone, who issued a preliminary injunction blocking DHS from carrying out its plans to erect a border barrier in the area, this is the border region with “the lowest aggregate number of apprehensions [of migrants] and the lowest number of apprehensions per mile of border.”

In Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church, a group of individuals with personal or business ties to the region, along with two advocacy groups, argued that DHS had failed to comply with required environmental reviews. Pointing to a 1996 law signed by President Bill Clinton, the Justice Department responded that Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and his predecessor, Kristi Noem, waived application of those environmental laws. The government also argued that the district court lacked the power to decide the lawsuit in the first place.

Cardone disagreed with the government on both counts. Congress narrowed courts’ jurisdiction in border-barrier disputes, but left room for courts to consider constitutional challenges to DHS’s conduct, she concluded. The challenge to Mullin’s waiver of environmental laws raises a constitutional question, Cardone added.

Having concluded that she could consider the challengers’ lawsuit, Cardone then turned to the criteria that Congress imposed on the secretary of Homeland Security to waive environmental review. The 1996 law directs the immigration agency “to waive all legal requirements” that could slow or impede construction of border barriers and roads. But the same law also instructs DHS to build barriers and roads “in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.” Considering the government’s data about apprehensions of people and seizures of drugs in the Big Bend Sector, as compared to other parts of the U.S.-Mexico border, Cardone concluded that the region cannot be considered to have high levels of illegal entry. “[I]f the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector,” Cardone announced.

Seven days after Cardone released her opinion, the U.S. solicitor general asked the Supreme Court to intervene. Much of the government’s argument turns on its disagreement with Cardone about what constitutes an area of “high illegal entry.” Mullin determined that the Big Bend Sector constitutes an area of high illegal entry because Customs and Border Protection, the DHS agency that enforces immigration laws at and near the border, apprehended 89,000 people and “seized enormous amounts” of illicit drugs from fiscal years 2021 to 2025, the government explains. In addition, failure to build a border barrier in this region “would act as a dangerous magnet” for additional illegal entries, the solicitor general claims. Despite Mullin’s assessment that the facts on the ground met the “high illegal entry” threshold required by Congress, “the district court nonetheless issued an unprecedented injunction blocking those waivers and halting associated border-wall construction,” the solicitor general wrote to the court.

Unsurprisingly, the challengers disagree. Opposing the government’s request for relief from the justices, they describe Mullin and Noem’s waivers as “unprecedented” and claim they “carry undisputed and extraordinary political and economic significance.”

The solicitor general’s claim is fundamentally a dispute about the proper interpretation of the text of the 1996 law. The government argues that courts cannot second-guess Mullin’s decision to waive environmental laws, and that Mullin’s view of what constitutes “high illegal entry” is all that matters. Cardone disagrees and contends that courts have a role to play here.

By turning to the emergency docket, the Justice Department has dispensed with the ordinary appellate process in favor of a fast-track path to, it hopes, final victory. Wanting an answer sooner rather than later is understandable, but a party’s interest in “line-jumping,” as Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson has described the emergency docket, isn’t reason enough to circumvent the slower course of the ordinary appellate process. Jackson would prefer to limit the emergency docket to situations in which an actual emergency exists. It’s hard to see what exigency exists in west Texas, however. The solicitor general argues that drugs and people will continue to enter through the Big Bend Sector. That is undoubtedly true, but, as that stretch of land has been unfortified since it became a border on March 18, 1848, nothing is likely to occur in the near future that is markedly different from past decades.

The government’s request for fast-track intervention by the Supreme Court also does not meet the standards set by Jackson’s ideological opposites. Explaining his view of the court’s emergency docket in Trump v. CASA, the court’s fast-track decision announcing that district courts are not authorized to issue universal injunctions, Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that its alternative pathway is appropriate when “Congress passes a major new statute, or the Executive Branch issues a major new rule or executive order.” Neither applies to the border-wall dispute. Congress enacted the contested statute 30 years ago and the waivers issued by Mullin and Noem are neither an agency rule nor an executive order.

Nor is the border-wall legal battle the type of dispute that only the Supreme Court can resolve. In a 2021 speech, Justice Samuel Alito compared the court’s emergency docket to a hospital’s emergency room, suggesting that, in his view at least, the fast-track process is proper only when no suitable alternative exists. But an alternative does exist to decide if Cardone overstepped. The government could have appealed Cardone’s decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit. Like other circuit courts, the 5th Circuit regularly reviews preliminary injunctions granted by district courts. As Kavanaugh explained in CASA, “The courts of appeals and this Court can (and regularly do) expeditiously review district court decisions awarding or denying preliminary injunctive relief.” Instead of asking the 5th Circuit to correct the mistake it claims Cardone committed, the solicitor general skipped the 5th Circuit and went directly to the Supreme Court.

The reason it did this is not difficult to figure out: The administration is hopeful that it will receive a friendly audience at the Supreme Court. But this is a fast-track procedure meant for exceptional circumstances. And there is nothing exceptional about the legal fight over the administration’s attempt to build new segments of border barrier in rural west Texas. If the court grants the government’s request to pause Cardone’s preliminary injunction, allowing construction to move forward where no barrier currently exists, it should, at the very least, explain how this case meets the criteria that the justices have previously provided and if the term “emergency docket” is a misnomer.

text:
Congressman Robert Garcia has spent his first years on the House Oversight Committee pushing for answers he has no power to compel. On Tuesday, voters could change that.

If Democrats win control of the House of Representatives in these midterm elections, the former Long Beach mayor is in line to chair the crucial committee, whose subpoena and investigative powers could put a check on the Trump administration.

In an interview Friday, Garcia said that if given the seat, he would launch investigations into alleged corruption within the Trump family and administration along with a gamut of other targets: allegations of pay-to-play in contracting with the Department of Homeland Security, congressional stock trading, corporate profiteering, and issues and delays with the release of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation files.

Among the first things Garcia says he would do with his newfound power is hold federal immigration agents accountable. This comes with increasing urgency after federal agents descended upon North Long Beach last month and detained a U.S. citizen, allegedly breaking his arm in the process.

Garcia has already written to the DHS inspector general demanding answers about what happened, but with Democrats in the minority, he can’t use the Oversight Committee’s powers to do much more. He can write letters, hold press hearings and question witnesses, but he can’t call hearings or compel testimony without Republican consent. He says Chairman James Comer has repeatedly canceled or stalled sessions and resisted bipartisan subpoena votes.

If he takes the majority chair, Garcia said he will investigate anyone “involved in the abuses of ICE,” to include the federal agents but also administrators who train them and “set the tone” for a culture of impunity.

“It can’t just be the agents,” Garcia said. “The agents are taking direction in some cases from others, and policy is being written to encourage that level of activity and that level of elimination of due process. Accountability at all levels, and that starts at the top.”

He plans to hold field hearings, starting early next year with one in Long Beach on “abuses of ICE and DHS.”

State Sen. Lena Gonzalez, a former Long Beach City Council member, said this is the top issue she and many others want to see addressed. At recent town halls and political rallies, ICE raids were top of mind for those in the crowd, regardless of party affiliation.

“Everyone nods their head, and they’re like, ‘Please do something,’” she said.

In a statement Monday, the local immigrant rights group ÓRALE said it is counting on Garcia “to follow through with his promise” to hold ICE agents accountable.

“People’s lives depend on this accountability,” the group stated.

A packed oversight agenda

Garcia said he also wants to focus on corporate corruption, on “any CEO that has been ripping off the American public,” that he thinks is linked to the nationwide affordability crisis.

This means taking otherwise opaque topics — cryptocurrency schemes, dynamic pricing, Jared Kushner and his conflicting interests as a businessman and U.S. peace envoy, and insider trading (by Congress members and the Trump administration alike) — and tying them to the tabletop issues, like groceries and gas prices.

“No one should be profiting off the people,” Garcia said. “We’ve got to restore trust with the American public, so that’s going to take really aggressive action early on.”

Sara Sadhwani, a political science professor, says Garcia could see a lot of success by tying issues of corruption and self-dealing by the Trump administration and framing it as an affordability concern.

“The Trump family is getting incredibly wealthy, while we, the American people, are struggling to make ends meet on a monthly basis,” she said.

But experts warn there are pitfalls in Democrats overextending themselves on their ambitions. Attempting to address too many topics from the jump can easily lead to problems.

Matt Lesenyie, a political scientist at Cal State Long Beach, said success will come from moving quickly on a handful of issues and “run[ning] them to a conclusion.” He listed Iran war casualties and “economic interventions that look like collusion” as possibilities.

Lesenyie said the public wants “action and accountability.”

Much of Garcia’s success could ride on Garcia’s own ability to keep the public engaged.

The congressman has, since joining the House Oversight Committee in 2023 and rising to minority chair last June, repeatedly fashioned himself a ubiquitous thorn in President Trump’s side.

With pomp and soapbox flair, he has led a sprawling investigation into the Justice Department’s handling of the Epstein files, called for cabinet resignations, and launched probes into federal immigration operations in Minneapolis and Los Angeles. Most recently, he sought to block Trump’s new $230 million ballroom.

He’s built a reputation and popularity around keeping the public interested in the topics he himself is interested in, untethered to the news cycle.

“He’s the guy who will be on MSNBC or CNN every single night talking about the Epstein files,” Sadhwani said. “He is keeping it in the minds of voters, and I’m curious to see with all of the possible avenues that he can go down, assuming he steps into this position, which ones will he really pursue, and which ones will he continue to hammer into the minds of voters.”

Sadhwani said Garcia is the right person for the job because he’s “an excellent communicator,” something that — in the social media ecosystem — has become just as important as managing investigations and pursuing legal remedies.

“It almost doesn’t even matter how much evidence you show,” Sadhwani said. “It’s about, you know, sadly, in this day and age, it’s about hitting their algorithm, you know. And I think the congressman seems to really understand that.”

It all hinges on Tuesday

The scale of what is possible for Garcia and Democrats still depends on their success in the midterms.

Currently, Republicans hold a narrow 218-214 majority in the House and a 53-47 majority in the Senate, with several vacancies due to resignations and deaths.

Democrats must defend their battleground seats and flip a number of Republican-held districts in tightly contested races nationwide, according to the Cook Political Report. Tight competitions are especially fraught in Kansas, Iowa, Maine and Texas.

If they take only the House, that may limit a lot of Garcia’s ambitions. If they take both sides of Congress, that could allow for a number of new ways to thwart the president, including the power to veto presidential actions and even a path — they still need enough votes — to impeach him for a third time.

“So much rides on Democrats’ ability to take the House, but also whether or not Democrats will have the ability to take the Senate,” Sadhwani said. “That’s a really big, wide-open question right now.”
