title: Is Donald Trump Preparing to Rule Without Congress – and Could America Be Heading ...
description:
What followed was one of the darkest episodes in modern American political history.
Many participants in the attack were subsequently prosecuted and imprisoned, although President Trump later issued sweeping pardons and commutations for January 6th defendants.
It can develop through a succession of apparently technical decisions that gradually weaken the institutions responsible for restraining executive power.
The fact that it happened once should make Americans particularly alert to the possibility of another confrontation between presidential ambition and constitutional authority.
The question facing America is no longer simply whether Donald Trump can govern without Congress.
text:
1.7K

There is a question that should be troubling every American who cares about the future of their democracy: what happens if Donald Trump decides that Congress is no longer an obstacle he needs to respect?

A Reuters investigation published on November 1st, 2026, raises precisely that concern. According to the report, the White House has spent months preparing ways to continue implementing Trump’s political agenda through executive authority should Democrats win control of Congress in the midterm elections. Senior figures, including presidential adviser Stephen Miller and budget director Russell Vought, are reportedly examining how presidential powers could be used to circumvent congressional opposition.

The areas under consideration reportedly include immigration, tariffs, housing and federal spending. The administration is also preparing for the prospect of congressional investigations into its activities, including possible claims of executive privilege to resist demands for information.

On one level, this is politics as usual. Every American president wants to advance his programme, and executive orders have long been used by administrations of both parties when Congress proves unwilling or unable to cooperate.

But there is a more disturbing dimension to this development. When does a president’s determination to bypass political opposition become an attempt to undermine the constitutional system itself?

And, more importantly, is Donald Trump contemplating something considerably more ambitious than simply governing without Congress?

The lessons of January 6th

Americans have already witnessed what can happen when Trump’s political ambitions collide with the constitutional machinery of government.

On January 6th, 2021, following his defeat by Joe Biden in the presidential election, thousands of Trump supporters descended on Washington. After a rally at which Trump repeated allegations that the election had been stolen, his supporters marched towards the Capitol.

What followed was one of the darkest episodes in modern American political history. The Capitol was breached. Members of Congress were forced to flee or seek shelter. The certification of the presidential election was interrupted as police officers fought to contain the violence.

The objective of the congressional proceedings was straightforward: formally certify Biden’s victory. Yet the process was disrupted by a mob acting in the name of a president who refused to accept his electoral defeat.

The subsequent congressional investigation documented Trump’s pressure on elected officials, his promotion of false election claims and his failure to act promptly to stop the violence. Many participants in the attack were subsequently prosecuted and imprisoned, although President Trump later issued sweeping pardons and commutations for January 6th defendants.

The significance of January 6th extends beyond the violence itself. It demonstrated that the peaceful transfer of power, a principle that had survived America’s civil war and numerous political crises, could be placed under extraordinary pressure by a sitting president. That history cannot simply be dismissed as an unfortunate episode from Trump’s first presidency.

Governing without Congress: a constitutional grey area?

The Reuters revelations raise legitimate questions about the boundaries of presidential authority.

The American Constitution deliberately divides power between the executive, legislative and judicial branches. Congress has the authority to enact legislation, approve federal spending, conduct investigations and exercise oversight over the executive. The president, meanwhile, is responsible for executing the laws passed by Congress. These are not administrative inconveniences. They are fundamental safeguards against the concentration of political power.

Trump’s apparent willingness to explore the limits of unilateral executive action suggests an administration preparing for confrontation with the legislature rather than compromise.

There is nothing inherently unconstitutional about a president using lawful executive authority. However, an administration cannot simply disregard legislation, appropriate money without legal authority or assume that presidential directives automatically override congressional statutes.

The courts remain an essential check on executive power, but what happens if the White House repeatedly tests those boundaries, challenges adverse judicial decisions and treats congressional oversight as illegitimate?

A constitutional crisis does not necessarily begin with tanks outside parliament or soldiers occupying government buildings. It can develop through a succession of apparently technical decisions that gradually weaken the institutions responsible for restraining executive power.

Is Trump planning to hold on to power?

There is an even bigger question. Trump is serving his second presidential term. The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution prohibits anyone from being elected president more than twice. His current term is therefore scheduled to end at noon on January 20th, 2029.

Could he nevertheless attempt to remain in power? There is currently no evidence in the Reuters report establishing that Trump is preparing a coup, planning to cancel elections or intending to refuse to leave office when his constitutional term expires.

It would be irresponsible to present such a conclusion as an established fact. Nevertheless, the possibility deserves scrutiny, particularly given the events of 2021.

Would Trump accept an electoral defeat for his party as a legitimate expression of the American electorate’s wishes? Would he accept a Democratic-controlled Congress investigating his administration? And, looking further ahead, would he accept the constitutional requirement to surrender the presidency in January 2029?

These are questions that should be answered through actions rather than assurances.

The distinction between governing aggressively and undermining democracy is an important one. But it is also a distinction that can become blurred when the executive repeatedly seeks to expand its authority at the expense of other constitutional institutions.

The danger of normalising the extraordinary

One of the greatest dangers facing American democracy is that extraordinary political behaviour can gradually become normalised.

If a president repeatedly challenges the authority of Congress, attacks judges who rule against him, dismisses independent institutions as politically motivated and portrays opponents as enemies of the state, the cumulative effect can be profoundly damaging.

The concern is not simply that Trump might issue more executive orders. It is whether the political culture surrounding his presidency is becoming increasingly intolerant of constitutional restraints.

There is also a distinction between winning an election and acquiring unlimited authority. Even a president with a substantial electoral mandate remains subject to the Constitution. The American system was designed precisely to prevent an individual from exercising unchecked power.

The midterm elections will therefore represent an important test of the relationship between the White House and Congress. A Democratic victory would not deprive Trump of his presidential powers, but it would restore an important mechanism of legislative scrutiny.

And that scrutiny is precisely what the constitutional system is supposed to provide.

America must not wait for another January 6th

Perhaps the most disturbing aspect of the present situation is that America has already experienced a serious attempt to disrupt the democratic transfer of power. January 6th was not an abstract constitutional debate. It was a physical assault on the institution responsible for certifying the outcome of a presidential election.

The fact that it happened once should make Americans particularly alert to the possibility of another confrontation between presidential ambition and constitutional authority.

It would be premature to declare that Trump is planning a coup. The Reuters investigation does not establish that. Governing through executive powers, even aggressively, is not in itself a coup. However, it would be equally complacent to dismiss every warning sign as merely another example of Trump’s unconventional political style.

The fundamental question is whether the president recognises that his authority is temporary, limited and ultimately subordinate to the Constitution.

A president who seeks to govern without congressional cooperation is exercising political power. A president who seeks to govern without constitutional constraints is attempting something altogether different.

A president who refuses to surrender power when his term expires would cross a line that no American president has the right to cross. America’s founding fathers understood the dangers of concentrated executive authority. They created a system of checks and balances because they understood that democracy depends not simply on who wins power, but on whether those who win are prepared to relinquish it.

The question facing America is no longer simply whether Donald Trump can govern without Congress. It is whether America’s institutions, its courts, its elected representatives and ultimately its citizens will be prepared to defend the Constitution if the president attempts to place himself above it.

text:
President Donald Trump has endorsed several Republican candidates who have publicly broken with him on key issues, prioritizing party unity as the GOP fights to maintain control of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Trump recently issued a "complete and total endorsement" for Representative Lauren Boebert of Colorado, months after disparaging her and threatening to pull his support during a dispute involving GOP Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky and files related to the late Jeffrey Epstein.

In Florida, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar has maintained Trump’s endorsement despite her public criticism of his immigration policies. In Iowa, Republican Senate nominee Ashley Hinson has similarly positioned herself as willing to challenge the administration on issues that affect voters in her state.

Read More on News

The president's endorsements highlight a strategic posture by Trump as Republicans face significant political headwinds. Historically, the president’s party loses seats in Congress during the midterms when his approval is low, and Trump’s approval has reached record lows in recent surveys. Issues like the economy, the cost of living and soaring gas prices amid the Iran war have driven the slip in his approval.

Control of the Senate remains a primary focal point. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority and are defending 22 of the 35 seats up for election. To seize control, Democrats must retain all 13 of their seats on the ballot and gain four seats currently held by Republicans.

Newsweek reached out to the White House, Boebert, Hinson and Salazar, as well as political analysts by email Sunday for comment.

Boebert Wins Trump's Backing After Public Clash

On Friday, Trump called Boebert an “America First Patriot” and a “MAGA Warrior” who was “doing an incredible job representing Colorado’s 4th Congressional District.” He added: “Lauren Boebert has my Complete and Total Endorsement for Re-Election. GET OUT AND VOTE FOR LAUREN — SHE WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!”

The president's endorsement of Boebert marks a turnaround from their dispute earlier this year when he called the congresswoman "dumb" and threatened to withdraw his support amid tensions over her campaigning for Massie , a leading critic of the administration's handling of Epstein-related records who was fighting a Trump-backed primary challenger. Massie ultimately lost his reelection campaign.

Boebert had supported efforts with Massie to force further disclosure of government records connected with Epstein, a convicted sex offender, putting her at odds with Trump during the dispute.

In a Friday afternoon X post, the congresswoman wrote that she "just finished a FANTASTIC Tele Rally with President Trump!" adding, "We’re going to win on Tuesday and SAVE AMERICA!"

As of October 23, Cook Political Report has Colorado's 4th Congressional District race classified as "Lean Republican" after it was previously listed as "Solid Republican."

Maria Elvira Salazar Criticized Trump's Immigration Policies

Salazar, who is seeking reelection in Florida's 27th Congressional District, has also publicly challenged Trump over a signature administration issue.

In September, the congresswoman broke with Trump over his immigration enforcement policies, saying in a campaign advertisement that the administration had gone "too far."

"Be careful about what your advisers are telling you about immigration policies," Salazar said. "The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."

Trump responded at the time to Salazar's ad with criticism but stopped short of withdrawing support.

"She obviously doesn't have a very strong feeling for the border, but I do," he told reporters. "She's a nice person. I got her elected. Without me, she wouldn't have gotten elected."

Trump also suggested Salazar had softened her views on immigration enforcement.

"She got a little bit soft on the border. I understand that. I understand that, but I just don't happen to be there," he said.

The president emphasized his continued commitment to strict border enforcement, arguing that immigration was central to his political success.

Still, Trump did not revoke the endorsement he gave Salazar earlier this year, when he praised her "Wisdom and Courage" and offered his "Complete and Total Endorsement."

As of September 25, Cook Political Report has Florida's 27th Congressional District race classified as "Lean Republican" after it was previously listed as "Likely Republican."

Ashley Hinson Balances Trump Backing With Independence

The balancing act is particularly consequential for Hinson who is running for the open Senate seat in Iowa.

Hinson won the Republican primary decisively in June, taking 74 percent of the vote against former state Senator Jim Carlin's 25.7 percent, according to certified results.

The seat is open because Republican Senator Joni Ernst is not seeking reelection. Iowa is among the Republican-held seats the Associated Press identifies as Democrats' best pickup opportunities, alongside Alaska, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas.

Trump endorsed Hinson's Iowa Senate bid in September, calling her a "winner" and a "loving wife and proud mother."

Recently, Hinson criticized Vice President JD Vance over his response to GOP criticism of Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial campaign ad featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic rival in the Ohio governor’s race.

The dispute escalated after Vance said he was "disgusted" by the Republican backlash against the advertisement, prompting Hinson to criticize his response as "ridiculous" and "the wrong tone."

Trump, who is campaigning for Hinson on Sunday, defended Ramaswamy's advertisement while also rebuking Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, who was among the Republicans criticizing it.

Hinson has also put distance between herself and Trump over the Iran war. In September, she called for the conflict to end during an affordability-focused press conference in Des Moines after previously opposing congressional efforts to impose limits on the war.

The disagreement was particularly significant because Hinson was campaigning in a state where the economic consequences of the conflict had become an election issue. Her comments linked the war to affordability concerns facing Iowans rather than representing a broader rejection of Trump's foreign policy.

Hinson has similarly sought to separate herself from administration policies affecting farmers, a politically important constituency in Iowa. Trump's beef policy has sparked anger among cattle producers in states where Republicans face competitive races.

She has also taken a harder public line against Trump's dealings with Russia, calling the president's diesel deal with Moscow a "bad idea" last month and saying she opposed deals with the country.

As of August 20, Cook Political Report has the Senate race classified as "Toss Up" after it was previously listed as "Lean Republican."

What Happens if Republicans Lose the Midterms?

Republicans losing control of either chamber of Congress would significantly constrain Trump's ability to advance his legislative agenda during the final two years of his presidency.

If Democrats recapture the House, they could block Republican legislation and use control of committees to launch investigations, issue subpoenas and increase oversight of the Trump administration.

Meanwhile, Democratic control of the Senate could make it significantly more difficult for Trump to confirm federal judges, Cabinet officials and other executive-branch nominees, and would give Democrats leverage over any Supreme Court vacancy that arose during the remainder of his term.

If Democrats retook both chambers, legislative gridlock would become much more likely. Democrats could pass their own legislation, but Trump could veto bills that reached his desk. However, Democrats would need to have the two-thirds majorities in both chambers needed to override presidential vetoes.

The loss of Congress for Republicans could therefore push the White House to rely more heavily on executive orders, emergency powers and regulatory actions to pursue the president's priorities, although those moves could face challenges in court.

A Democratic takeover could also revive discussion of impeachment, which has split some members of the party. The House has the sole power to impeach a president by a simple majority, although removing Trump from office would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate, a threshold Democrats are not positioned to reach on their own.

text:
Immigration advocates are suing the state of Tennessee, arguing a new policy is unfairly preventing some non-U.S. citizens who are here legally, from obtaining temporary driver's licenses.

The lawsuit challenges changes made by the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security that advocates say could leave thousands of immigrants unable to drive — despite having federal permission to be in the United States.

Under the previous policy, Tennessee accepted work permits and other federal documents as proof of legal authorization to remain in the country.

But advocates say the state is now limiting the types of documents certain noncitizens can use to qualify for a temporary driver's license.

Under the new requirements, applicants must present a valid visa, an I-94, an I-94W or a temporary green card.

That leaves some people who have held Tennessee driver's licenses for years, or even decades, suddenly being denied when they attempt to renew.

RELATED COVERAGE | ICE: Man arrested outside Nashville airport known or suspected Tren de Aragua gang member

"Under its new rule, TDOS will only issue driver's licenses to certain non-citizens who present a valid visa, an I-94 or an I-94W or somebody with a temporary green card," said Jazmin Ramirez, advocacy director for the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition.

"As a result, people who have held a driver's license for years or even decades are now being turned away and denied renewals for the first time."

The Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition filed the lawsuit, arguing the policy excludes people who have federal authorization to live and work in the United States.

Immigration attorney Kathleen Martinez says the state is effectively treating people with work permits as if they do not have authorized immigration status.

"They're treating everyone with a work permit as if they are not here with authorized stay," Martinez said in a post on social media.

DACA recipients among those affected

During a virtual news conference, advocates described how the changes are affecting immigrants who depend on their ability to drive to work, take their children to school and handle everyday responsibilities.

DACA recipients are among those potentially impacted. Many have federal work authorization but are not issued the specific immigration documents Tennessee now requires.

One person who spoke during the news conference, but asked to remain anonymous, described how losing their license has affected their job.

"Currently, I am employed at a Level 1 trauma center but cannot show up to work because I am without a license and live an hour away," the person said.

Advocates say the consequences could extend to thousands of people who previously qualified for temporary licenses but no longer meet the state's revised documentation requirements.

Lawsuit questions state's authority to make changes

The lawsuit argues Tennessee officials implemented the new restrictions without following the proper legal procedures.

Attorneys contend the Department of Safety and Homeland Security overstepped its authority by changing which federal documents are accepted and failed to give the public an opportunity to weigh in before the policy took effect.

The legal challenge comes after Tennessee passed sweeping immigration legislation that went into effect this year.

State officials have reportedly interpreted the new law as allowing the department to impose stricter requirements for temporary driver's licenses.

However, advocates argue the state cannot use the legislation to deny licenses to people who have otherwise been authorized to live and work in the country under federal law.

The lawsuit asks the court to intervene and challenge the state's new licensing requirements.

WZTV reached out to the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security for comment.

The department responded that it does not comment on ongoing litigation.

title: A Pregnant Haitian Woman Faces an Uncertain Future After Trump Ends Temporary Protected Status
authors: Fhrynée Pierre-Lambert, Ava Slocum, Gloria L. Blackwell
description:
Eight months pregnant, after suffering a miscarriage in August 2025, she was navigating a high-risk pregnancy complicated by avascular necrosis, a condition that eventually led to a double hip replacement.
This was meant to be one of the happiest moments of her life, and seven months ago, it might have been.
For pregnant Haitian women like Marie, the consequences reach the most ordinary acts of preparing for a baby.
“I feel so bad for her sometimes… I’m sorry that I’m bringing her into this world under these circumstances.
It feels like somehow failing in life.” At 30, Marie had imagined a different future for herself.
text:
For one expectant mother, the end of Temporary Protected Status has turned prenatal care, childbirth and the future she imagined for her daughter into sources of fear and uncertainty.

Marie (a pseudonym) lay on the cold examination table again, watching as the doctor moved the ultrasound wand across her belly. Eight months pregnant, after suffering a miscarriage in August 2025, she was navigating a high-risk pregnancy complicated by avascular necrosis, a condition that eventually led to a double hip replacement. Now, as she listened to her baby girl’s heartbeat, she couldn’t help but wonder whether the receptionist had frowned at her because she was having a bad day or because something in Marie’s file had made her consider calling U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

This was meant to be one of the happiest moments of her life, and seven months ago, it might have been. Seven months ago, she had health insurance. Seven months ago, she was a pharmacy technician preparing to go to medical school and a community organizer encouraging people to get involved in local government. Now, she was among the estimated 350,000 Haitians who had lost their Temporary Protected Status (TPS) after the Trump administration terminated Haiti’s designation on July 27, 2026, following a U.S. Supreme Court ruling that cleared the way for the termination.

She wondered how much it would cost to stay healthy enough to give birth.

High-risk OB-GYN appointments: $90.

Ultrasounds and maternal-fetal medicine: $340 a month.

Prescribed prenatal vitamins: $290 a month.

What about the delivery? Her doctor has told her there’s a 90 percent chance she’ll need a C-section because of her condition and recovery from the double hip replacement, Marie says. What if she just skipped the doctor’s appointments this next month? Can her baby girl afford that risk?

The end of TPS means more than losing an immigration status. It threatens people’s ability to work, maintain health insurance, pay bills and support their families. For pregnant Haitian women like Marie, the consequences reach the most ordinary acts of preparing for a baby. Going to a doctor’s appointment, paying medical bills and planning for delivery can all become financial risks they can no longer afford to take. Fears of immigration enforcement have also left pregnant immigrants across the country weighing the risks of seeking medical care.

As I sat with Marie, I watched as she held back tears when she spoke about her daughter and the guilt she felt. “I feel so bad for her sometimes… I’m sorry that I’m bringing her into this world under these circumstances. It feels like somehow failing in life.”

At 30, Marie had imagined a different future for herself. “One day you are law-abiding, you’re paying your taxes, you’re doing what you’re supposed to do in this country. And the next day they’re saying you’re illegal. It’s not right,” says Marie.

As she spoke about where her life stood now, the gap between what she had planned and what she was facing became clear.

For pregnant people, the uncertainty created by the end of TPS makes it harder to imagine a future without calculating what might be taken away. Is it safe to go to the hospital? Is it safe to go to the grocery store? Can I afford groceries and rent? If I return to Haiti, will I be safe? Will I ever see my family again?

For Marie, these questions are especially urgent. With her due date fast approaching, even imagining the months ahead has been difficult. “I’m just thinking about getting through with delivering the baby right now,” she explains. “I think that’s as far as I can think forward.”

Despite having big dreams for the future, Marie’s focus has narrowed to getting through her pregnancy. The uncertainty surrounding her future has also taken an emotional toll, one that became clear as she spoke about her life at 30.

“Yesterday felt so long. I stayed in bed for almost 12 hours yesterday. I had no energy to get up. And I cried, and I couldn’t understand why I was crying. I know that I’m pregnant and there’s hormones involved, but for someone like me who’s taken my professional career very seriously, to feel like this at this moment in time when I just turned 30, I’m about to have a baby, and this is what my life looks like right now.”

Marie’s exhaustion is not unique within the Haitian community. Earlier this month, the community buried Pierre Damas Bel, a 20-year-old Haitian college student who died by suicide on Aug. 31 after losing TPS and being required to wear an ankle monitor by ICE.

Bel, who had recently begun studying at Wright State University, had spoken about the shame and humiliation he felt wearing the monitor. His family said the experience, along with bullying and fear of deportation, contributed to his despair. His death has deepened the grief and fear of a community already confronting the financial and emotional consequences of an uncertain future.

I asked Marie what she hoped for her daughter. Rubbing her belly, she said, “I would love for her to grow up in a world where she’s not going to experience the things that I’m experiencing … Being a community organizer, I’ve seen change happen in my lifetime, so I know it is possible for things to change. Nothing can stay the same. I’m hopeful that the generation that we are in will help turn the boat around.”

One measure currently before Congress, Senate Bill 4814, would require the federal government to designate Haiti for TPS through April 20, 2029, giving eligible families additional time to plan their futures without fear of deportation. Introduced in June, the legislation remains in the Senate Judiciary Committee and has not advanced to a floor vote.

Marie’s daughter is not yet here, but her future is already entangled with politics, uncertainty and decisions being made far beyond her mother’s control.

With the Nov. 3 midterm elections approaching, voters have an opportunity to examine where candidates stand on Temporary Protected Status, immigration enforcement and access to healthcare for immigrant families.

These aren’t abstract policy debates for people like Marie. They’re questions of whether a mother can afford prenatal care, whether she can work to support her family and whether she can imagine a secure future for her daughter.

*

A note from Ms. editors: We want to hear from you for The Majority, a new campaign collecting stories about how reproductive freedom has enabled readers to build the lives they want and need.

text:
Seats on the highest courts in Texas — the state Supreme Court, the Court of Criminal Appeals and the newer 15th Court of Appeals — are up for grabs in this year's midterm election. Texas voters will choose which jurists sit on courts that shape state law on issues like child welfare, death sentences and elections themselves.

All members of these courts are elected statewide in partisan races. Judges appointed by Republican Gov. Greg Abbott currently hold seven of the 10 seats up for election across all three courts.

Democrats are looking to regain ground in the courts, which have been Republican strongholds for decades.

Texas Supreme Court

The Texas Supreme Court is the state's court of last resort in civil matters. It handles cases involving child custody, divorce, constitutional challenges to state laws, wrongful death lawsuits and other issues via appeals from lower courts.

The court has nine justices who serve staggered six-year terms. There's no term limit for these positions.

Those appointed to their seats by the governor are required to run for official election to their position in the following election cycle. This year, those candidates are incumbent justices James "Jimmy" Blacklock, James Sullivan and Kyle Hawkins.

The court has made important rulings on hot-button issues, such as the criminalization of delta-8 THC, abortion access, gay marriage and gender-affirming care.

Chief Justice

Jimmy Blacklock (R, incumbent)

Appointed to the court in 2018 and named chief justice in 2025, Blacklock previously served as Abbott's general counsel and as an attorney in the Texas Attorney General's Office. He's argued cases involving religious liberty, federalism and election law, and has authored more than 100 opinions on the court. Blacklock describes his judicial philosophy as grounded in interpreting statutes and the state constitution according to their text and original meaning.

Maggie Ellis (D)

Ellis serves on Austin's Third Court of Appeals and is board certified in juvenile law. With more than 15 years in legal practice, she has worked as a prosecutor, administrative law judge and trial attorney handling civil, juvenile and family cases. She is the first openly LGBTQ+ woman ever elected to a Texas appellate court.

Justice, Place 2

James Sullivan (R, incumbent)

Appointed to the Texas Supreme Court in 2025, Sullivan previously served as Abbott's general counsel. Earlier in his career, he clerked in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Washington, D.C., Circuit and worked in the Texas Attorney General's Office and private practice. He has also taught as an adjunct professor.

Chari Kelly (D)

Kelly serves on the Third Court of Appeals in Austin, where she has been on the bench since 2019. A U.S. Army veteran and former Judge Advocate General officer, she has ruled on cases involving public health, environmental issues and criminal justice. Before joining the court, she worked on litigation for the state and taught trial advocacy at the University of Texas School of Law.

Justice, Place 7

Kyle Hawkins (R, incumbent)

Appointed to the court in 2025, Hawkins previously served as Texas solicitor general and as counselor to the U.S. solicitor general under President Donald Trump. He has argued multiple cases before the U.S. Supreme Court and previously clerked for Justice Samuel Alito. Hawkins also worked in private appellate practice and taught at the University of Texas School of Law.

Kristen Hawkins (D)

Kristen Hawkins is a Harris County district court judge first elected in 2016. She has experience in civil litigation, including medical malpractice, construction and mass tort cases, and is double board certified in civil trial and personal injury law. She has chaired judicial committees in Harris County and received recognition for her work on complex litigation matters.

Justice, Place 8

Brett Busby (R, incumbent)

Appointed in 2019 and elected statewide in 2020, Busby previously served on the Texas Court of Appeals for six years. A former U.S. Supreme Court law clerk, he has argued cases before appellate courts across the country and has taught at the University of Texas School of Law.

Gisela Triana (D)

Triana serves on the Third Court of Appeals and previously spent more than two decades as a trial court judge in Travis County, presiding over both civil and criminal matters. She began her legal career as a prosecutor and has also worked in election law and private practice.

Texas Court of Criminal Appeals

The Court of Criminal Appeals is Texas' highest court for criminal cases, including death penalty appeals.

The court has nine judges who serve staggered six-year terms. There's no term limit for these positions.

The court has weighed in on the ongoing appeal of Robert Roberson, who was convicted of murder after prosecutors successfully argued for his conviction in part with controversial "shaken baby syndrome" evidence.

The court also made an important ruling that found the Texas attorney general can not unilaterally prosecute voter fraud claims — a ruling that led Ken Paxton to back three judges who ousted incumbents in 2024.

The only judge who sided with Paxton in the voter fraud case was Kevin Patrick Yeary, who's also the only incumbent on the Court of Criminal Appeals ballot this year.

Judge, Place 3

Thomas Smith (R)

Smith works in the Texas Attorney General's Office and previously served as counsel to then Senator Ken Paxton. He began his career in private practice and clerked for a state supreme court justice in Ohio. His experience includes criminal justice and government litigation.

Okey Anylam (D)

Anyiam is a Dallas-based criminal defense attorney who has been licensed in Texas since the late 1990s.

Judge, Place 4

Kevin Patrick Yeary (R, incumbent)

Elected to the Court of Criminal Appeals in 2014, Yeary previously worked as an appellate prosecutor in several large Texas counties and served as a briefing attorney at the court early in his career. He has argued cases before the Texas Supreme Court and the U.S. Supreme Court.

Audra Riley (D)

Riley serves as judge of Dallas County Criminal District Court No. 3, a position she has held since January 2021. Her current term on that court runs through 2028. She earned her law degree from the Thurgood Marshall School of Law and has experience presiding over felony criminal cases in one of the state's largest counties.

Judge, Place 9

John Messinger (R)

Messinger works in the Office of the State Prosecuting Attorney and has filed more than 100 petitions for discretionary review with the Court of Criminal Appeals. He frequently speaks at statewide criminal law conferences and chairs a State Bar criminal jury charges committee.

Holly Taylor (D)

Taylor is a criminal appellate attorney and former prosecutor who most recently served in a leadership role in the Travis County District Attorney's Office, overseeing public integrity and complex crimes divisions. She is board certified in criminal appellate law and previously worked as a staff attorney at the Court of Criminal Appeals.

15th Court of Appeals

Created controversially by the Legislature in 2023, the 15th Court of Appeals has statewide jurisdiction over certain cases involving the state itself and business disputes.

The court has three justices who serve six-year terms.

This is the first year anyone on the Abbott-appointed court is up for election. The statewide jurisdiction of this intermediary court means it's touched on a number of notable cases in its short existence.

A Bloomberg Law analysis in July found the state wins the majority of contested cases the 15th Court of Appeals has decided. Most recently, the court sided with Abbott in a dispute with Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, pressing pause on a trial court judge's order requiring Abbott to let Hinojosa view emails between the incumbent governor and Elon Musk.

But the court has also dealt some blows to state officials, including striking down Paxton's rule requiring large-county district attorneys to send detailed reports to his office and the attorney general's failed attempt to overturn the State Fair of Texas' gun ban.

Chief Justice

Scott Brister (R, incumbent)

Appointed as the inaugural chief justice in 2024, Brister previously served on the Texas Supreme Court and on Houston-area appellate courts. He has presided over hundreds of trials and authored hundreds of appellate opinions. In private practice, he led appellate litigation at a large firm.

Jerry Zimmerer (D)

Zimmerer previously served on the 14th Court of Appeals in Houston before losing reelection in 2024. He has worked in private practice and in corporate legal roles, including with AT&T Mobility.

Justice, Place 2

Scott Field (R, incumbent)

Appointed to the 15th Court of Appeals in 2024, Field previously served on the Third Court of Appeals and as a district court judge in Williamson County. He has practiced commercial and appellate litigation and clerked at the Texas Supreme Court.

Tom Baker (D)

Baker is a former justice on the 5th Court of Appeals who lost reelection in 2024. A U.S. Navy veteran, he now works in private practice in Central Texas.

Justice, Place 3

April Farris (R, incumbent)

Farris was appointed to the 15th Court of Appeals in 2024 after serving on the 1st Court of Appeals. She previously worked as an assistant solicitor general for Texas and as a partner in private practice handling complex appellate litigation. She has received national recognition for her appellate work.

Marc M. Meyer (D)

Meyer is an attorney, registered nurse and retired Houston firefighter. He lives in Montgomery and has experience in both public service and private legal practice.

Additional reporting by KERA's Emmanuel Rivas Valenzuela.

text:
A Canadian-born dentist in Minnesota is no longer facing an immediate deportation order, his lawyer says, but he's still in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody.

ICE detained William Lizardo on Oct. 23 during a green card interview in downtown Minneapolis. It came as a shock to the Lizardo's wife, Lauren, that he had a deportation order hanging over his head. The couple was unaware, they said, because the federal government sent them a critical "notice to appear" before a judge to an address in Virginia that they hadn't lived at for more than two years.

According to court filings, an immigration court has now determined that Lizardo missed the appearance through no fault of his own. In granting Lizardo's motion to reopen the in absentia order from March, the judge found "Respondent has provided sufficient evidence demonstrating his lack of notice."

Hassan Ahmad, Lizardo's immigration attorney now working on the case, said that it's clear that the government made an error. He's now working to get Lizardo home, because he argues that ICE no longer has justification for keeping him detained.

"If the government can detain and deport somebody based on inauthentic paperwork the way that they are trying to do in this case, then nobody has any hope," Ahmad said.

Court records show that ICE is still attempting to find a way to force Lizardo out of the country. Once ICE responded to WCCO's initial inquiry about the issue following his detainment, which took the agency five days to do, it said that Lizardo had "overstayed his lawful entry."

Ahmad said that this isn't true, arguing that Lizardo has a legal right to remain in the country while he pursues a green card. Lizardo was initially denied a green card in January, but he filed an immediate appeal within the legal window, according to Ahmad.

Lauren Lizardo is hoping to see her husband home soon as she looks after their 18-month-old daughter.

"I want to be treated with compassion and kindness. I feel like I haven't been given that opportunity and Will hasn't either," Lauren Lizardo told WCCO the day that her husband was detained.

Lizardo is still behind bars in Sherburne. ICE has not acknowledged WCCO's inquiry submitted on Friday.

title: Federal judge orders ICE and Border Patrol to stop racial profiling - NPR
description:
Transcript AYESHA RASCOE, HOST: A federal judge in Los Angeles says there's overwhelming evidence immigration agents roving the streets of Southern California have been violating the Constitution.
NPR's Adrian Florido joins us now from Los Angeles.
RASCOE: Adrian, this is the second time this judge has issued this ruling.
He wrote that immigration agents can consider race, along with other factors, to suspect that someone is in the country illegally.
They also filed declarations from dozens of Latinos who were detained by immigration agents, including U.S. citizens wrongly detained.
text:
Transcript

AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:

A federal judge in Los Angeles says there's overwhelming evidence immigration agents roving the streets of Southern California have been violating the Constitution. They've been racially profiling, she found, detaining people for deportation just because of what they look like. NPR's Adrian Florido joins us now from Los Angeles. And note - we will hear a racial slur in this conversation. Adrian, thanks for being with us.

ADRIAN FLORIDO, BYLINE: Hi, Ayesha. Thanks.

RASCOE: Tell us what this federal court has found.

FLORIDO: Well, the judge, Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong, said it very simply. She said that ICE and Border Patrol agents have, quote, "engaged in an unlawful, officially sanctioned practice of detaining individuals solely based upon their appearance as Latino or Latino and working class" (ph). The judge said that she was convinced by mountains of evidence that the ACLU and other civil rights groups presented in court to prove that agents out rounding people up have been racially profiling, and she ordered ICE and Border Patrol to stop its agents from doing that.

RASCOE: Adrian, this is the second time this judge has issued this ruling. Last year, the Supreme Court tossed out her first one. So why is she doing it again?

FLORIDO: Well, last year's order, Ayesha, was a temporary one based on limited evidence, and the Supreme Court tossed it out without offering a reason. The only hint as to why came from a concurrence that Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote. He wrote that immigration agents can consider race, along with other factors, to suspect that someone is in the country illegally. But that ruling did not end the underlying lawsuit here. And so since then, the ACLU has, in this case, gathered a lot of evidence to convince the LA judge that immigration agents have been using race, not as one factor, but as the only reason to stop people. This is Mohammad Tajsar, one of the ACLU's lawyers in the case.

MOHAMMAD TAJSAR: They know nothing about people other than the fact that they're brown and they look like they're working class. And based on those two broad demographic characteristics, armed goons descend on them and stop them and kidnap them.

RASCOE: Tell me more about this evidence that convinced the judge that that's true.

FLORIDO: Well, the government handed this evidence over after the judge in the lawsuit ordered it to. And there were text messages in which agents used racial slurs. Lawyers got to depose immigration agents. They also filed declarations from dozens of Latinos who were detained by immigration agents, including U.S. citizens wrongly detained. There was also body cam footage, Ayesha. Like this video, you can hear two agents who've just raided a Home Depot parking lot.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

UNIDENTIFIED AGENT #1: I checked one guy's ID.

UNIDENTIFIED AGENT #2: Did you?

UNIDENTIFIED AGENT #1: Yeah.

UNIDENTIFIED AGENT #2: There's a guy. I'm pretty sure he's wet. He was just sitting in that minivan.

FLORIDO: He says he's pretty sure that a man he saw in a minivan was wet, and that is short for wetback, a racial slur for Latino immigrants. In terms of enforcement, all this judge's preliminary injunction this week does is tell agents to stop detaining people just because they look Latino, and it gives the lawyers a tool to ask for sanctions if the government keeps doing this.

RASCOE: This ruling only applies in seven counties in Southern California, including Los Angeles, but could it have ramifications elsewhere in the country?

FLORIDO: Well, the ACLU's attorney thinks that, yes, that the ripple effects could be national because LA is not the only place where immigration agents are accused of racial profiling. This is the ACLU's Mohammad Tajsar again.

TAJSAR: It will have an impact not just on how the government conducts its operations throughout the country, but also on how communities respond and prepare their own cases and are themselves becoming more vigilant.

FLORIDO: The Department of Homeland Security, Ayesha, has always denied that its agents racially profile. We asked for a comment on this ruling and did not hear back. The agency did, though, file an appeal this week, and this case is likely to end up again before the Supreme Court.

RASCOE: That's NPR's Adrian Florido. Thank you so much for joining us.

FLORIDO: Thank you, Ayesha.

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

JEFFERSON CITY — Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, alongside Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach, is leading a 22-state coalition supporting proposed federal rule changes that would exclude unauthorized immigrants and temporary foreign visitors from the population totals used to apportion congressional seats and Electoral College votes.

The proposed regulatory revisions, published jointly by the U.S. Department of Commerce and the U.S. Census Bureau, would adjust the agency’s traditional “usual residence” counting standards. Under the proposal, only U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents would be counted within the apportionment base that determines each state’s share of seats in the U.S. House of Representatives. The proposed framework also seeks public comment on reintroducing citizenship and legal residency questions to the decennial census questionnaire ahead of 2030.

“Election integrity requires fair representation based on the American people—not political power gained by counting illegal immigrants and temporary foreign visitors,” Hanaway said. “This commonsense rule would help ensure that illegal immigration cannot sway the census, distort congressional apportionment, or dilute the representation of law-abiding states.”

In public comments submitted on behalf of the coalition, the attorneys general argued that congressional representation should reflect lawful, permanent status rather than simple geographic presence. The coalition recommended that beginning with the 2030 Census, every household should be directly asked to verify whether each resident is a U.S. citizen and, if not, whether they hold lawful permanent resident status.

The joint effort follows legal action brought by Hanaway’s office against the Census Bureau earlier this year challenging the counting of undocumented populations during decennial reapportionments. Hanaway contended that counting unauthorized populations transfers federal legislative clout from interior states to coastal jurisdictions with large non-citizen populations. State officials cited economic and demographic analysis suggesting that counting unauthorized immigrants allowed California to retain three additional congressional seats following the 2020 enumeration, while Missouri was denied an additional legislative seat and electoral vote.

“States should not receive additional congressional representation as a reward for encouraging illegal immigration,” Hanaway said. “We’re glad the Trump Administration has renewed efforts to restore constitutional representation in Congress. We will not allow non-citizens to game the census and cheat our system for political power.”

In addition to Missouri and Kansas, state officials from 20 other states joined the comment letter: Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, and West Virginia.

text:
Federal immigration agents have fanned out across California’s Central Valley in recent weeks, stirring fear in Latino communities and allegations of voter intimidation in a toss-up race that could help decide control of the US House of Representatives.

The planned surge in California was announced to agents in early October, an internal email seen by Reuters shows. And it was directed by the White House, according to a US official, speaking on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

Unlike past operations in big cities like Minneapolis and Chicago that put hundreds of armed, masked agents on the streets, the surge here has been characterized by small groups of officers moving from town to town in the largely agricultural region. The United Farm Workers union said it knew of hundreds of California farmworkers detained in recent weeks.

In Bakersfield, immigration arrests jumped from one a day for much of the year to nearly 10 per day in mid-October, according to preliminary Department of Homeland Security data. In nearby Wasco, home to just 26,000 people, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested at least seven people in the span of a few days, the data showed.

The arrests have caused widespread alarm in the Latino-majority areas – and could have implications for Tuesday’s midterm elections, in which Republicans will be fighting to retain control of the House and Senate.

In California’s 22nd congressional district, which includes Bakersfield and is 73% Latino, polls have shown progressive Democrat Randy Villegas with a slight edge over six-term Republican incumbent David Valadao.

Villegas told reporters last week that the arrests were a “very clear attempt to try and intimidate our communities before this election.”

Valadao said in a statement that he understood “the fear and uncertainty immigration enforcement has created for families throughout our communities,” urging the Trump administration to “prioritize the removal of individuals who pose a threat to public safety.”

The DHS, ICE’s parent agency, declined to comment on the California operations, citing concerns for officer safety, and did not respond to the allegations of voter intimidation.

“By all metrics, this should be a very close district,” said Thad Kousser, co-director of UC San Diego’s Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections. “Anything that drives voters to or away from the polls could matter.”

President Donald Trump made historic inroads with Hispanic voters in the 2024 election, but polls show public opinion has turned sharply against his immigration sweeps and economic policies.

Just 24% of Hispanic Americans approve of Trump’s performance, the lowest share in either of his presidential terms, a Reuters/Ipsos survey found last month.

In a statement, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said that Trump’s agenda had made Hispanic Americans “more prosperous and safer” and referred questions on ICE operations in California to DHS.

Climate of fear

Across the Central Valley, ICE has made arrests outside homes and at busy intersections, in strip mall parking lots, gas stations and near schools, according to lawyers, immigration advocates, videos and court records.

“Agents were given the green light to be out and make as many arrests as possible,” the US official said. Officers are also auditing records at local businesses and using employee information to arrest workers at their homes or on their daily commute, the official added.

Maribel Ramirez, a local farmworker, said the arrests have had a chilling effect on political activity in the area. She said that some young Hispanics with US citizenship have told her they are scared to vote, fearing it could expose the addresses of family members without legal status.

Even though voter information is meant to be private, some of “those who can vote won’t do so because their parents are immigrants,” she said.

Ramirez is urging every US citizen she knows to cast a ballot, “but not for anyone in red,” referring to Republicans.

Immigration activists in the area who have been sharing alerts about ICE sightings on social media are also, in some cases, sharing details about the midterm elections.

There are fewer people on the streets in Bakersfield, according to Ana Valencia, who owns a barber shop in town. Some local businesses are offering free delivery to those afraid to leave their homes.

Valencia says she voted early “because I don’t want ICE here, or anywhere really.”

Villegas has made the arrests a campaign issue, criticizing his opponent for voting to triple ICE’s budget and failing “to stand up for immigrant communities.”

Valadao has said ICE is targeting criminals in the community. In an interview with the Sacramento Bee published this week, he said the agency had gone too far in some cases but declined to give examples.

Jason Giannelli, 41, a fourth-generation farmer in Kern County who supports Valadao, said the Republican was “middle of the road” on immigration and “understands that probably ICE is going after the worst of the worst.”

Farmworkers targeted

UFW national Vice President Elizabeth Strater told Reuters that the vast majority of farmworkers detained in recent weeks had no criminal records and some had legal work authorization.

A brother and sister from Mexico were unloading their shopping in a small town in Kern County in late October when immigration agents arrested them, a relative told Reuters, speaking on the condition of anonymity.

It was their day off from work in the fields nearby.

The agents were looking for someone else and did not know whom they had picked up until the handcuffs were on, according to a petition filed by the farmworkers’ lawyers in federal court contesting their detention as unlawful.

The sister arrived in the US as an unaccompanied minor more than a decade ago, according to the petition. The brother arrived as a toddler. Neither has criminal records, the petition says.

DHS said it did not have enough information to comment on the case.

On the day of the arrest, the woman’s 3-year old daughter was at daycare and her 11-year-old son was on a school camping trip. The children’s father had died suddenly this year, leaving their mother as the sole caregiver.

The 11-year-old returned home excited to see his mother, the relative said. When he heard she had been arrested, he broke down in tears and cried out for her.

The 3-year-old perks up whenever the phone rings, the relative said, asking if her mother is on the line.

text:
The death toll in Immigration and Customs Enforcement facilities keeps climbing, but there is one glaring problem with that news: major media outlets have stopped reporting on it.

Despite two deaths occurring in ICE detention centers in the past month, the silence across mainstream media outlets has prompted a much louder question:

How many deaths does it take for a national media corporation to deem the occurrence newsworthy?

Apparently, that number is higher than the 57 deaths that have been reported since President Donald Trump took office again.

Luis Sandoval and Roberto Jimenez Gutierrez died in Georgia’s Folkston facility on Oct. 23 and California’s Otay Mesa facility on Oct. 24, respectively.

Despite press releases from ICE on the individual deaths, there was little to no media coverage.

Daily Kos combed through CNN, NBC, and ABC’s web sites looking for reports on the two men, but found that only local stories and one international outlet—The Guardian—covered just Sandoval’s death.

Related | Inside the fight to protect immigrants as deaths surge in ICE prisons

This, combined with ICE’s already loosened reporting requirements, makes for a dangerous pattern of unreported deaths.

“People are dying in ICE custody across the country,” Rebecca Brown, supervising attorney at Public Counsel, told Daily Kos in a written statement.

“These deaths are not isolated tragedies or local stories. They are the predictable result of a detention system that holds more people than ever while failing to provide basic medical care and humane treatment,” Brown said.

Public Counsel is a nonprofit public interest law firm that works on many immigration cases, including a focus on the Adelanto ICE facility in Southern California. As we’ve previously reported, Public Counsel is in a legal brawl with the Trump administration in order to secure safe conditions for immigrants being held there.

As it stands, reports of mold and gnat larvae in the showers, dirty drinking water, and deteriorated living conditions are still being reported within the facility despite court orders ruling its past treatment of immigrants unconstitutional.

At least four people have died at Adelanto.

And this drop in coverage by large national outlets doesn’t come at the decrease of violence and deaths at the hands of the agency, but rather the opposite.

In addition to thedeaths inside the walls of privately and federally owned facilities, agents have been blasted for thecontinued abuse and shootings of immigrants they sought to detain.

Federal agents have killed nine people and injured 13 others in a total of at least 30 shooting events since the start of Trump’s second term, according to reporting by CBS.

The public outrage that tends to influence national coverage has not lessened either.

In fact, hacktivists who call themselves the Department of Peace recently released approximately 41,000 names, emails, phone numbers, and work addresses of workers within the Department of Homeland Security, including ICE agents.

And protests are still filling streets across the country.

But the bigger picture as mainstream media turns its back on these stories contains a dark truth: With less media coverage comes the likelihood of less public pressure.

“When these deaths stop making the news, the government faces even less pressure to stop them,” Brown told us. “Every one of them deserves national attention.”

title: ICE activity motivates voters in competitive California congressional race - CSMonitor.com
authors: Cindy Carcamo, The Christian Science Monitor
description:
Here, in California’s competitive 22nd Congressional District, the most heavily Latino district in the state, there is concern over recent immigration enforcement.
It has triggered protests and accusations that the Trump administration is trying to scare Latino voters.
Though the courts blocked its implementation, an increase in naturalization and a shift among Latino voters toward the Democratic Party followed.
He says it can be scary to walk the streets near dusk because of recent ICE activity, but he puts that feeling aside.
But because of recent ICE actions in town, some are too afraid to come to the door.
text:
Before federal immigration agents surged in California last year, Marisol Perez wasn’t interested in politics. But when the Trump administration’s immigration dragnet swept the state – in some cases, detaining people with legal status and even U.S. citizens – she paid attention.

Ms. Perez, a teenager, watched the flood of social media images and videos of masked federal agents handcuffing and taking away people who frequently looked like her or her relatives, she says.

Then, a few weeks ago, Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials descended on her town of Wasco, a farming community of about 26,000 people. Local police say they are aware of at least two immigration enforcement incidents in the community, though they have not confirmed how many people were detained.

Now, just months after her 18th birthday, Ms. Perez is eager to vote in direct response to what she’s seeing in her community.

Here, in California’s competitive 22nd Congressional District, the most heavily Latino district in the state, there is concern over recent immigration enforcement. In some cases, canvassers encounter people who will not answer the door because they fear who might be knocking. But in places like Wasco, there are signs that the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown could also motivate voters.

“I need to vote for the people who can’t vote,” Ms. Perez says.

A political shift

In Wasco, one of several farming communities in the San Joaquin Valley, locals describe a sudden spike in immigration enforcement in the weeks leading up to the election. It has triggered protests and accusations that the Trump administration is trying to scare Latino voters.

It was an anti-immigrant push that helped turn California blue more than two decades ago. In 1994, a ballot initiative passed that would have barred unauthorized immigrants from public services and forced state employees to report those suspected of not having legal status. Though the courts blocked its implementation, an increase in naturalization and a shift among Latino voters toward the Democratic Party followed.

Nationally, there has been pushback to President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, an issue that helped return him to the White House two years ago. A Fox News poll in September found 53% of registered voters say the administration’s immigration enforcement has gone too far. Polling also indicates that Mr. Trump has lost significant support among Latinos who backed him in 2024, though a majority of those voters continue to approve of his performance.

Today, California’s 22nd District – one of several redrawn last year to give Democrats an edge in response to gerrymandering in Republican-controlled states – is hotly contested. Republican Rep. David Valadao is seeking reelection against Democrat Randy Villegas. It is one of several races that could allow Democrats to retake control of the House. Mr. Valadao’s district was redrawn to now include parts of the large inland city of Fresno, bringing more Democratic voters into Mr. Valadao’s district.

Flor Olvera, who has spent weeks canvassing for Democratic-leaning candidates in her hometown of Wasco, says fear is palpable in her community. But she says the federal immigration surge in town – where 87% of the population is Latino – is actually moving many voters she’s spoken with to take action.

“Some people may feel hesitant to vote because they fear they may be racially profiled on their way to the polls,” she says. “But more than anything, I’m actually seeing more momentum to vote.”

“Operation Safe California”

Mr. Villegas, the son of Mexican immigrants, has accused the Trump administration of suppressing Latino voters and condemned the federal immigration sweeps.

His opponent, Mr. Valadao, whose family migrated from Portugal, has expressed concern about fear among immigrant farmworkers and reiterated his support for a pathway to legal status for longtime residents. But he also said in a statement posted on his U.S. House website that he’s been in contact with federal officials regarding the recent immigration enforcement, and they’ve said that “these operations are focused on individuals with active warrants and known criminal histories.”

That might – or might not – be the case.

The Washington Examiner, a conservative news outlet in D.C., reported that unnamed sources familiar with the plan said they intended to arrest people they encountered in California without legal status, including those without a criminal record, as part of a 45-day push called “Operation Safe California,” which began in October.

In an unsigned statement to the Monitor, the Department of Homeland Security declined to “disclose or discuss law enforcement operations.”

“Every day, DHS enforces the laws of the nation across the country, including in California,” the statement said.

Federal immigration agents have spent weeks scouring the Central Valley, immigrant rights organizers say, noting warrantless arrests and the targeting of farm laborers on their way to work.

Ms. Perez, who lives with noncitizen family members, says she’s also trying to persuade her classmates at the local college to vote for Mr. Villegas – meaning against Mr. Valadao, who has supported the Trump administration’s increased ICE funding.

“It’s just not right,” she says.

Nuanced views, support for tighter borders

The newly redrawn 22nd Congressional District covers portions of Kings, Kern, Fresno, Madera, and Tulare counties. It is now more Democratic-leaning than it was when Mr. Valadao last won.

The district’s Latino electorate is predominantly young, working-class, and migratory – a demographic that historically tracks lower in voter turnout, according to several studies. This has created challenges for Democratic candidates.

Also, Latino conservatives hold unique, nuanced views on immigration, according to extensive polling by the Pew Research Center and the UCLA Latino Policy & Politics Institute.

Data shows the majority of Latino Republicans favor increased border security. More than 30% of Hispanic Republicans also support increasing deportations of people who are in the country illegally as a policy priority, according to a 2022 Pew survey.

Marco Florez, a board member of the Central Valley Young Republicans who was born and raised in Exeter in Tulare County, says he supports the recent ICE enforcement.

“For me, being a Latino doesn’t mean I support open borders,” Mr. Florez says. “Security comes first.”

Mr. Florez says he understands mistakes may have been made by ICE agents, who have arrested and detained people who are in the U.S. legally.

“Sometimes, people are wrongfully arrested. I don’t deny that fact,” he says.

But those mistakes, he says, are eventually sorted out, and people are released.

“I don’t think this is going to strain the Latino vote by any means,” he said of the ICE actions.

Motivation

Elizabeth Chur, who is canvassing for Mr. Villegas in the 22nd District, says that “especially, young people are motivated in a way that I have not seen before in previous election cycles.”

Ms. Chur, a San Francisco resident, has canvassed in Wasco and surrounding areas since 2018.

A grassroots voter-engagement trainer and author of the guidebook “The Joy of Talking Politics with Strangers: How to Save Democracy, One Conversation at a Time,” Ms. Chur says U.S. citizen voters who live in mixed-status households are particularly motivated by recent ICE arrests in their communities.

That’s the case for Gabriel, who just turned 18 and lives in Lamont.

Gabriel, who did not give his last name because his mother lacks U.S. residency, says he not only plans to vote but is actively encouraging others to do the same.

On a recent evening, Gabriel hit the streets of the Kern County farming community of Arvin to distribute leaflets. One was in both English and Spanish.

“I want to do my part for my community,” says Gabriel, who works for Faith in the Valley, a faith-based, grassroots community group in California’s Central Valley that advocates racial, economic, and environmental justice.

He says it can be scary to walk the streets near dusk because of recent ICE activity, but he puts that feeling aside.

“The fear is there. I don’t think it will ever go away,” he says. “But I don’t stop just because of that fear.”

Normally, Gabriel would knock on doors and ask people to vote. But because of recent ICE actions in town, some are too afraid to come to the door.

So, he leaves information on their front stoops or on a chain-link fence. The leaflet explains people’s rights and includes a long list of tips for “when you vote” and “if immigration agents come.”
